Some ecologists [[argue]] that cities can serve as refuges for certain bird species.
partners: argue that / argue for / argue against
uses: In answer choices: "The author argues that the policy benefited cities more than rural areas."

meaning: To stop or check the progress of a process, such as a disease, a decline or a spread.
examples: Replanting the hillsides with grass helped [[arrest]] the erosion that had been swallowing the village's fields.
Doctors hoped the new drug would [[arrest]] the infection before it reached the lungs.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Wardens trying to catch the poachers noticed something else: the fence built to keep the poachers out had also [[arrested]] the spread of an invasive grass, which now stopped abruptly at the wire.
nearly.clue: which now stopped abruptly at the wire

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The sheriff blamed counterfeiters for the town's troubles, but it was the new bank, not the sheriff, that [[arrested]] the town's decline: once it began issuing sound notes, prices steadied and shops reopened.
nearly.clue: prices steadied and shops reopened

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: A sudden shout from the doorway [[arrested]] the girl's hand just as she reached for the letter, and she stood frozen, her fingers an inch from the envelope.
nearly.clue: she stood frozen, her fingers an inch from the envelope

partners: arrest a decline / the spread of

lookalikes.tell: Arrest means stop a process; wrest means pull something away by force.

meaning: Striking and eye-catching; so interesting or unusual that it holds attention.
examples: The cover shows an [[arresting]] image: a single red boot standing in the snow.
Her essay opens with an [[arresting]] claim that most readers will want to dispute.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The detective novel opens with an [[arresting]] scene: a woman walks into a police station carrying a birdcage and asks to confess.
nearly.clue: a woman walks into a police station carrying a birdcage

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Among the telescope's first pictures was an [[arresting]] view of two galaxies colliding, their spiral arms twisted into long glowing streams.
nearly.clue: their spiral arms twisted into long glowing streams

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The mural's most [[arresting]] figure, a sheriff holding a lantern, was painted larger than any other and placed at the very center.
nearly.clue: was painted larger than any other and placed at the very center

lookalikes.tell: Arresting means striking and eye-catching; alarming means frightening or worrying.

meaning: To express an idea or feeling clearly in words.
examples: In her 1848 speech, Stanton [[articulated]] demands that many listeners had never heard stated in public.
uses: In answer choices: "It articulates the principle that the rest of the text applies to specific cases."

meaning: To find out something for certain, usually by checking or investigating.
examples: Using tree rings, the researchers were able to [[ascertain]] the exact year the cabin was built.

lookalikes.tell: Ascertain means find out for sure; assert means state confidently.

meaning: To have a strong hope or ambition to achieve something.
examples: Like many young writers of her era, she [[aspired]] to publish in the national magazines of New York.
partners: aspire to a career / to become

lookalikes.tell: Aspire means aim for something yourself; inspire means move someone else to act or feel.
Aspire means aim high; expire means end or run out.

meaning: To express agreement with or approval of a proposal or request.
examples: Only after the council had [[assented]] to the plan could construction on the new bridge begin.
partners: assent to a plan / a request

lookalikes.tell: Assent is agreement; an ascent is a climb upward.

meaning: To make a claim with confidence, whether or not it is proved.
examples: The article [[asserts]] a connection but offers little evidence.

lookalikes.tell: Assert states a claim; assess evaluates it.

uses: In answer choices: "The author asserts that the policy was a failure but offers little evidence."

meaning: To evaluate the quality, amount, or significance of something.
examples: The panel will [[assess]] the proposal against published criteria.

lookalikes.tell: Assess evaluates a claim; assert states one.

meaning: To make an unpleasant feeling, such as fear, guilt, or hunger, less intense.
examples: The company released its safety data in an effort to [[assuage]] the fears of nearby residents.

lookalikes.tell: Assuage means soothe a feeling; persuade means convince.

meaning: To accept something as true without checking or proving it.
examples: Early mapmakers [[assumed]] that the river flowed from a great inland lake, but no such lake existed.

meaning: To take on a role, duty, responsibility or appearance.
short: take on a role or duty
examples: After her husband's death, Hatshepsut [[assumed]] the powers of a pharaoh and ruled Egypt for two decades.
In the second act, the heroine [[assumes]] a disguise and returns to the court as a servant.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: When the governor fell ill, the council did not simply suppose that his deputy would lead; it voted, and the deputy [[assumed]] command of the colony the next morning.
nearly.clue: command of the colony the next morning

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: In a hive that loses its queen, some worker bees [[assume]] a new role: their ovaries develop, and they begin laying eggs of their own.
nearly.clue: their ovaries develop, and they begin laying eggs of their own

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The quiet clerk [[assumed]] an air of great importance whenever the manager left the room, straightening his collar and speaking to customers in a deeper voice.
nearly.clue: straightening his collar and speaking to customers in a deeper voice

lookalikes.tell: Assume means take on a role; resume means begin again after a pause.

meaning: So surprising that it is hard to believe.
examples: The probe returned [[astonishing]] images of ice volcanoes on a moon once thought to be frozen solid.

lookalikes.tell: Astonishing describes the thing that surprises; astonished describes the person who is surprised.

meaning: Quick to notice and understand things, especially in a way that gives an advantage.
examples: An [[astute]] observer of politics, Tocqueville noticed tensions in American democracy that its own citizens overlooked.

lookalikes.tell: Astute means shrewd; acute usually means severe, as in an acute shortage.

meaning: To reach or achieve something, usually through effort.
examples: Few of the early colonies [[attained]] the self-sufficiency their founders had promised investors.
partners: attain a goal / a level / independence

lookalikes.tell: Attain means reach a goal or level; obtain means get possession of something.
Attain means achieve; retain means keep.

meaning: To say that something results from a particular cause or belongs to a source.
examples: The report [[attributes]] the decline to changing rainfall patterns.

lookalikes.tell: Attribute identifies a source; contribute adds to a result.

meaning: Showing a willingness to take bold risks; daring.
examples: The [[audacious]] mission called for landing a small probe on a comet moving at tens of thousands of miles per hour.

lookalikes.tell: Audacious means daring; audible means loud enough to be heard.

meaning: To make something greater by adding to it.
examples: Archival records [[augment]] the evidence from interviews.

meaning: Suggesting that future success is likely; favorable.
examples: The strong first harvest was an [[auspicious]] start for the new farming cooperative.

lookalikes.tell: Auspicious means promising good things; suspicious means distrustful, or arousing distrust.

meaning: Severely plain, with no decoration, luxury, or comfort. Of a person, it means stern and strict.
examples: The monks lived in [[austere]] cells furnished with only a cot, a stool and a candle.

lookalikes.tell: Austere is the adjective (plain, strict); austerity is the noun, often a government cutting its spending.
Austere means stern or plain; auspicious means promising good things to come.

meaning: Actually what it claims to be; not fabricated or imitated.
examples: The curator sought an [[authentic]] letter from the artist.

lookalikes.tell: Authentic means genuine; authoritative means accepted as reliable.

meaning: Trustworthy and reliable because it comes from a recognized expert or source.
examples: For decades her field guide remained the most [[authoritative]] source on North American mosses, cited in nearly every later study.

lookalikes.tell: Authoritative means reliable and expert; authoritarian means demanding strict obedience to power.

meaning: To give official permission for something.
examples: In 1803 Congress [[authorized]] funds for an expedition to map the lands west of the Mississippi.

lookalikes.tell: To authorize is to permit; to author is to write or create.
Authorize means give permission; authoritative means reliable or commanding.

meaning: Able to act or make decisions independently.
examples: The region gained an [[autonomous]] council with local authority.

lookalikes.tell: Autonomous means self-governing; automatic means operating with little human control.

meaning: Strongly disliking or unwilling to do something; usually followed by "to."
examples: Investors [[averse]] to risk tend to prefer government bonds over young technology firms.

lookalikes.tell: Averse describes a person who dislikes something; adverse describes conditions or effects that are harmful.

meaning: To prevent something bad from happening. It can also mean to turn one's eyes away.
examples: Quick action by air traffic controllers [[averted]] a collision over the crowded airport.

lookalikes.tell: Avert means head off something bad; divert means change the course or direction of something.
Avert is a verb meaning prevent; overt is an adjective meaning done openly.

meaning: Very eager and enthusiastic about something.
examples: An [[avid]] beetle collector, the young Darwin once put one in his mouth to free his hands for another.

lookalikes.tell: Avid means eager; vivid means bright or lifelike.
Avid means eager; arid means very dry.

meaning: Completely confused; unable to understand or explain something.
examples: Doctors were [[baffled]] by the illness, which struck only the village's oldest residents.
The detective remained [[baffled]] until he noticed that every clock in the house had been stopped at noon.

lookalikes.tell: Baffled means completely confused; babbled means talked rapidly and foolishly.

uses: In answer choices: "The researchers are baffled by results that contradict every earlier study."

meaning: To give appropriate attention to two or more competing needs.
examples: The essay tries to [[balance]] historical detail with narrative pace.
partners: balance X with Y / competing needs

lookalikes.tell: Balance weighs competing needs; ballast supplies stabilizing weight.

meaning: So ordinary and overused that it is dull and unoriginal.
examples: Reviewers praised the actors but found the dialogue [[banal]], full of lines they had heard a hundred times.

lookalikes.tell: Banal means dull and trite; a bane is a cause of ruin or misery.
Banal means dull; venal means open to bribery.

meaning: Coming or happening later than it should have.
examples: Rosalind Franklin's part in discovering the structure of DNA received [[belated]] recognition long after her death.

lookalikes.tell: Belated means late; bloated means swollen.
Belated means overdue; berated means scolded angrily.

meaning: Hostile and eager to fight or argue.
examples: The ambassador's [[belligerent]] remarks alarmed neighbors who had hoped the border dispute could be settled peacefully.

lookalikes.tell: Belligerent means eager to fight; beleaguered means under attack or heavy pressure.

meaning: Puzzled or confused, often mildly; it does not mean amused.
examples: The villagers watched, [[bemused]], as the scientists lowered microphones through holes in the frozen lake.
Her [[bemused]] expression suggested she had not understood a word of the explanation.

lookalikes.tell: Bemused means puzzled; amused means entertained. A bemused reader is confused, not laughing.

uses: In answer choices: "The narrator is bemused by her neighbors' elaborate rules for the shared garden."

meaning: Likely to help or improve a situation.
examples: Regular rainfall is [[beneficial]] to the restored wetland.

lookalikes.tell: Beneficial describes a helpful effect; benevolent describes kind intent.

meaning: Kind and generous, wanting to do good for others.
examples: The town's [[benevolent]] founder left most of her fortune to build a free public library.

lookalikes.tell: Benevolent describes a kind person or intention; beneficial describes a helpful effect.

meaning: Lacking knowledge or understanding; kept in ignorance.
examples: The reformer's letters describe the villagers as [[benighted]], a judgment that says more about his prejudices than about their lives.

lookalikes.tell: Benighted means unenlightened; knighted means given the rank of knight.
Benighted means ignorant; benign means kindly or harmless.

meaning: Harmless and gentle in effect; in medicine, not cancerous.
examples: Most of the bacteria living on human skin are [[benign]], and some even protect against more dangerous microbes.

lookalikes.tell: Benign means harmless in effect; benevolent means actively kind and wishing to help.

meaning: A natural talent for something or a tendency toward it; often used as “a bent for.”
examples: From childhood she showed a scientific [[bent]], collecting beetles and labeling every one.
Readers with a philosophical [[bent]] will enjoy the novel's long digressions.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The old gardener, whose back was crooked from years of work, recognized the boy's [[bent]] for growing things and gave him a corner of the greenhouse.
nearly.clue: for growing things and gave him a corner of the greenhouse

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Grace Hopper's mechanical [[bent]] showed early: as a girl she took apart alarm clocks to see how they worked.
nearly.clue: as a girl she took apart alarm clocks to see how they worked

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The reformer had a practical [[bent]]: rather than write about poverty, she opened a kitchen that fed four hundred people a day.
nearly.clue: rather than write about poverty, she opened a kitchen

partners: a bent for / a scientific bent

meaning: To give something, such as an honor, gift, or right, to someone.
examples: The academy [[bestowed]] its highest medal on the engineer whose dams had brought water to millions.
partners: bestow an honor / a title on

lookalikes.tell: Bestow means give as an honor; stow means pack or store away.

meaning: To reveal something without meaning to, such as a feeling, a secret or an origin.
examples: Her calm voice [[betrayed]] none of the fear she felt.
The slight tremor in his hands [[betrayed]] how nervous he was.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Though he swore loyalty to the duke, the steward's glance toward the door [[betrayed]] his wish to be gone.
nearly.clue: his wish to be gone

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The ice core looked uniform to the eye, but its chemistry [[betrayed]] a sudden warming about 12,000 years ago, when the levels of certain isotopes jumped within a few decades.
nearly.clue: when the levels of certain isotopes jumped within a few decades

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The spy never confessed, but the notes sewn into his coat [[betrayed]] his true purpose in the capital.
nearly.clue: the notes sewn into his coat

lookalikes.tell: Betray means reveal without meaning to; portray means depict on purpose.

meaning: A tendency to favor one view or group that can distort judgment.
examples: The sampling method introduced a [[bias]] toward urban households.

lookalikes.tell: Bias skews judgment; basis is the foundation for a claim.

meaning: Unimpressed or unconcerned because of having seen or done something many times.
examples: Having flown dozens of times, the young pilot was [[blasé]] about the takeoff, while his first-time passenger gripped the armrests.

meaning: Very obvious and done openly, with no attempt to hide something bad.
short: done openly, without trying to hide it
examples: The judge called the contract a [[blatant]] attempt to get around the new labor law.

lookalikes.tell: Blatant means openly obvious; latent means present but hidden or not yet active.
Blatant means glaringly obvious; bland means mild and dull.

meaning: Unpromising or severe in outlook or condition.
examples: The report painted a [[bleak]] picture of the harvest.

lookalikes.tell: Bleak means grim and without hope; bland means mild and dull.

meaning: To develop well and grow into something successful or impressive.
examples: The small trading post [[blossomed]] into a busy city once the railroad arrived.

lookalikes.tell: Blossom means develop and flourish; balloon means swell quickly, often out of control.

meaning: To make a boundary, image, or distinction hard to perceive.
examples: The broad category can [[blur]] differences among the species.

meaning: To make a claim, effort, or structure stronger.
examples: The newly found diaries [[bolster]] the historian's account.

lookalikes.tell: Bolster provides support; bluster is loud empty talk.

meaning: Genuine and real; not fake or pretended.
examples: Critics dismissed the diary as a forgery, but handwriting experts confirmed it was a [[bona fide]] record kept by a Civil War nurse.

lookalikes.tell: Bona fide is an adjective meaning genuine; bona fides is a noun for the credentials that show someone can be trusted.

meaning: Bold and shameless; acting openly without the embarrassment one ought to feel.
examples: The forger's [[brazen]] attempt to sell a fake Rembrandt to the museum that owned the original was quickly exposed.

lookalikes.tell: Brazen means shamelessly bold; a brazier is a pan for holding hot coals.

meaning: A failure to obey an agreement, rule, or duty.
short: violation of a rule or trust
examples: Publishing the private letters was a [[breach]] of the agreement.

lookalikes.tell: Breach is a violation; broach means introduce a topic.

meaning: Hard but easily broken or cracked. Said of things like peace or confidence, it means fragile.
examples: Cold temperatures made the ship's steel hull [[brittle]], so it cracked instead of bending.

lookalikes.tell: Brittle means easily broken; a bristle is a stiff hair, and to bristle is to react angrily.

meaning: To expand the range or extent of something.
examples: The new archive may [[broaden]] the study beyond one city.

lookalikes.tell: Broaden increases scope; burden places a weight or duty on someone.

meaning: Beginning to develop and showing early promise.
examples: The workshop gave [[budding]] scientists their first chance to present research to experts.

meaning: Cheerful and optimistic. Literally, able to stay afloat; said of an economy, rising and strong.
short: cheerful and upbeat; able to float
examples: Despite the poor harvest, the letters she sent home that autumn were [[buoyant]] and full of plans.
partners: a buoyant mood / buoyant spirits / a buoyant economy

lookalikes.tell: Buoyant is the adjective (cheerful, or floating); a buoy is a floating marker, and to buoy is to lift up.

meaning: To grow or expand quickly.
examples: The city's population [[burgeoned]] after gold was discovered nearby, doubling in just three years.

lookalikes.tell: Burgeon means grow quickly; bludgeon means beat with a heavy club.
Burgeon means grow; burden means weigh down.

meaning: To strengthen or support an argument, claim, or position.
examples: She [[buttressed]] her argument with census records showing how the neighborhood had changed.

lookalikes.tell: Buttress means strengthen an argument; bluster means talk loudly and aggressively to little effect.

meaning: To persuade someone to do something through flattery, gentle pressure, or repeated coaxing.
examples: The organizers [[cajoled]] reluctant local merchants into sponsoring the town's first public library.

meaning: Showing an insensitive, cruel disregard for other people's feelings or suffering.
examples: Reformers condemned the mill owners' [[callous]] indifference to the children working their looms.

lookalikes.tell: Callous means unfeeling; a callus is a patch of hardened skin.

meaning: Young and lacking experience or maturity.
examples: The [[callow]] young officer, only months out of school, made mistakes that his seasoned sergeant quietly corrected.

lookalikes.tell: Callow means immature and inexperienced; callous means unfeeling toward others.

meaning: Openly truthful, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
examples: In a [[candid]] interview, the artist described her failed early work.

lookalikes.tell: Candid means frank; candied means preserved with sugar.

uses: In answer choices: "The speaker's tone is candid, admitting mistakes openly."

meaning: The quality of being open and honest in what one says, even when the truth is unwelcome.
examples: Historians value the general's letters for their [[candor]] about the army's early defeats.

lookalikes.tell: Candor is the noun (honesty); candid is the adjective (honest and direct).

meaning: The ability to do, hold, or produce something.
examples: The museum lacks the [[capacity]] to preserve every artifact.
partners: the capacity to / at full capacity

lookalikes.tell: Capacity can mean available ability or room; capability is an ability to do a task.

meaning: Changing mood or behavior suddenly and without reason; unpredictable.
examples: Farmers in the valley learned to plant early, since the spring weather there was notoriously [[capricious]].

lookalikes.tell: Capricious means unpredictable; capacious means roomy.

meaning: Attracting and holding attention through charm or interest.
examples: The documentary's footage of hunting spiders was so [[captivating]] that even viewers who feared spiders could not look away.

lookalikes.tell: Captivating means charming and absorbing; captive means held prisoner.

meaning: To portray someone or something with certain features exaggerated, often to mock them.
examples: Rather than answer her opponents' arguments, the columnist [[caricatured]] them as greedy villains who cared nothing for the town.

lookalikes.tell: Caricature exaggerates features in order to mock; characterize simply describes typical qualities.

uses: In answer choices: "The author caricatures the opposing view in order to dismiss it."

meaning: Something that starts or speeds up a significant process.
examples: The discovery became a [[catalyst]] for wider reforms.

lookalikes.tell: A catalyst prompts change; catalysis is the process it prompts.

meaning: To cause or speed up a process or change. In chemistry, to speed up a reaction without being used up.
short: spark or speed up a change
examples: The publication of the report [[catalyzed]] a nationwide movement to clean up the rivers.

lookalikes.tell: Catalyze means spark or speed up a change; analyze means examine closely.
Catalyze means set a change in motion; catalog means make a list of items.

meaning: Careful attention to possible risks or mistakes.
examples: The author treats the uncertain dates with [[caution]].

meaning: To give up control of something, such as land, power, or a point in an argument, often unwillingly.
short: give up (land, power, or a point)
examples: Under the 1848 treaty, Mexico [[ceded]] a vast northern territory to the United States.

lookalikes.tell: Cede means hand something over; secede means formally withdraw from a nation or group.
Cede means give up; seed means plant, or a plant's seed.

meaning: To praise or honor someone or something publicly; in a text, to present an achievement with admiration.
examples: The poem [[celebrates]] the ordinary labor of fishermen and farmers.
Her obituary [[celebrated]] her work bringing clean water to rural towns.
uses: In answer choices: "The passage celebrates the achievements of the first women hired as astronomers."

meaning: Famous and widely praised.
examples: Long before she became a [[celebrated]] novelist, Cather worked as a magazine editor in New York.

lookalikes.tell: Celebrated means famous; cerebral means intellectual.

meaning: Relying on thought and reason rather than emotion or feeling; intellectual.
examples: Her early poems are [[cerebral]] puzzles; only in later collections does she write openly about grief.

lookalikes.tell: Cerebral means intellectual rather than emotional; celebrated means famous and praised.

meaning: To question whether a claim or idea is true or valid.
examples: The discovery of older tools in Chile [[challenged]] the theory that people first reached the Americas 13,000 years ago.
uses: In answer choices: "It challenges a common assumption about how the species migrates."

meaning: To fight for or publicly defend a cause, a person or an idea.
examples: Frances Perkins [[championed]] a minimum wage long before Congress was ready to pass one.
The botanist [[championed]] the use of native plants in city parks.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Few legislators in 1890 would speak for the eight-hour workday, but Senator Reade [[championed]] it in speech after speech, insisting that shorter hours would make workers healthier.
nearly.clue: insisting that shorter hours would make workers healthier

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: When other ecologists dismissed the idea that wolves could reshape rivers, Hayes [[championed]] it, collecting two decades of streambank data in its defense.
nearly.clue: collecting two decades of streambank data in its defense

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: At the county fair, where the Whitfield boys had won every ribbon for years, it was little Clara who [[championed]] the shy newcomer, telling every judge that his calf was the finest there.
nearly.clue: telling every judge that his calf was the finest there

meaning: In complete disorder and confusion.
examples: Eyewitness accounts of the evacuation describe a [[chaotic]] scene, with carts blocking every road out of the city.

lookalikes.tell: Chaotic means disordered; cathartic means emotionally releasing.

meaning: To describe the typical qualities of someone or something.
examples: Critics at the time [[characterized]] her paintings as crude, but today they are praised for their bold color.

lookalikes.tell: Characterize describes something's qualities; caricature exaggerates them to mock.

uses: In answer choices: "The author characterizes the policy as well meant but poorly planned."

meaning: To hold back, slow or limit something.
examples: The new dam [[checked]] the floods that had destroyed the lower valley every spring.
Each branch of government is meant to [[check]] the power of the others.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Foresters who inspected the burned hillside found that the fire break had [[checked]] the blaze: the flames reached the cleared strip and went no farther.
nearly.clue: the flames reached the cleared strip and went no farther

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The framers of the Constitution wanted each branch of government to [[check]] the others, so that no single official could gather too much power.
nearly.clue: so that no single official could gather too much power

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Clara opened her mouth to answer the insult, then [[checked]] herself, remembering that her mother was watching from the porch.
nearly.clue: remembering that her mother was watching from the porch

partners: check the spread / check one's anger / checks and balances

lookalikes.tell: Check means hold back; checkered means marked by ups and downs, as in a checkered past.

meaning: Lasting a long time or recurring often; usually said of a problem or illness.
examples: The report blamed the region's [[chronic]] water shortages on decades of overpumping.

lookalikes.tell: Chronic means long-lasting; a chronicle is a record of events in order.

meaning: To record a series of events in the order they happened.
examples: Her diaries [[chronicle]] the family's journey west, from the first river crossing to the final winter in Oregon.
partners: chronicle the rise of / chronicle events

lookalikes.tell: Chronicle means record events in order; chronic means long-lasting.
To chronicle is to record events; a chronology is the ordered list itself.

uses: In answer choices: "The passage chronicles the rise of the steel industry in Pittsburgh."

meaning: Careful to consider all risks and consequences before acting or speaking.
examples: Aware that censors might read her letters, the diplomat was [[circumspect]] about what she wrote.

lookalikes.tell: Circumspect means careful; circumscribe means limit, or draw a line around.
Circumspect means cautious; circumstantial means based on indirect evidence.

meaning: To find a way around an obstacle or rule, often cleverly or dishonestly.
short: get around a rule or obstacle
examples: To [[circumvent]] the blockade, merchants shipped their goods to a neutral port and then carried them overland.

lookalikes.tell: Circumvent means get around; circumscribe means draw a limit around, or restrict.

meaning: Kept secret or done secretly, especially because it is illegal or forbidden.
examples: Members of the resistance held [[clandestine]] meetings in a bakery cellar, far from the eyes of the occupying soldiers.

meaning: To remove uncertainty or confusion from an explanation.
examples: The final paragraph helps [[clarify]] the study's main claim.

lookalikes.tell: Clarify makes clear; classify sorts into groups.

uses: In answer choices: "It clarifies a term that the previous sentence uses without defining."

meaning: To come together and form a single group or whole.
examples: Over millions of years, dust and gas [[coalesced]] into the planets of the solar system.

lookalikes.tell: Coalesce means come together; coerce means force someone to act.
Coalesce means merge; convalesce means recover from illness.

meaning: To gently and patiently persuade someone to do something.
examples: The researchers spent weeks [[coaxing]] the shy birds to feed from their hands.

lookalikes.tell: Coax means gently persuade; a hoax is a trick meant to fool people.

meaning: To make someone do something by using force or threats.
examples: The workers testified that they had been [[coerced]] into signing the contracts under threat of losing their homes.

meaning: Clear, logical, and convincing.
examples: The lawyer's argument was so [[cogent]], each point backed by records, that the jury reached a verdict within an hour.

lookalikes.tell: Cogent describes a convincing argument; cognizant means aware of something.

meaning: To think deeply and carefully about something.
examples: The philosopher would [[cogitate]] on a single question for weeks before writing a word.

lookalikes.tell: Cogitate means think deeply; agitate means stir up or disturb.
Cogitate is the verb for thinking hard; cognition is the mental process of knowing.

meaning: Clear and consistent because the parts fit together.
examples: The notes yielded a [[coherent]] account of the expedition.

lookalikes.tell: Coherent means intelligible as a whole; cohesive means holding together.

meaning: To invent a new word or phrase.
examples: The German zoologist Ernst Haeckel [[coined]] the word “ecology” in 1866.
A reporter [[coined]] the phrase “Dust Bowl” to describe the drought-stricken plains.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The Treasury had just begun to mint a new silver dollar when a newspaper editor [[coined]] a nickname for it that stuck for decades.
nearly.clue: a nickname for it that stuck for decades

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The astronomer Fred Hoyle, who doubted the theory, is said to have [[coined]] the term “Big Bang” during a 1949 radio broadcast.
nearly.clue: the term “Big Bang”

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Dickens so often [[coined]] memorable names for his characters that some, such as “scrooge,” became ordinary English words.
nearly.clue: became ordinary English words

partners: coin a term / a phrase / a word

meaning: To happen at the same time as something else, or to match it closely.
examples: The two surveys [[coincide]] on the direction of the change.

lookalikes.tell: Coincide means agree or occur together; collide means strike each other.

meaning: To cooperate on a shared task or goal.
examples: The scientists will [[collaborate]] on a new map of the reef.

lookalikes.tell: Curious means eager to know more; cursory means hasty and shallow.

meaning: Strange or unusual in a way that draws attention.
examples: Collectors prize the coin for a [[curious]] flaw: the king's crown was stamped upside down.
It is a [[curious]] fact that the poet, famous for her sea verses, never once saw the ocean.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Researchers eager to understand the frogs noticed something [[curious]]: every animal in the pond was female, although the species normally hatches in equal numbers of each sex.
nearly.clue: although the species normally hatches in equal numbers of each sex

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Among the governor's papers is a [[curious]] letter, written in French, unsigned and addressed to a man who, by every other record, had died ten years earlier.
nearly.clue: addressed to a man who, by every other record, had died ten years earlier

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The children, who wanted to know everything about the new lodger, reported one [[curious]] habit above all: he ate his breakfast standing up, facing the wall.
nearly.clue: he ate his breakfast standing up, facing the wall

partners: a curious fact / a curious detail

lookalikes.tell: Curious here means strange; a curio is a small, unusual object collected for display.

meaning: Done quickly, without attention to detail.
examples: A [[cursory]] reading of the diary suggests a happy childhood, but a closer look reveals signs of hardship.

lookalikes.tell: Cursory means hasty; cursive is joined-up handwriting.

meaning: To cut short or reduce something, such as a right, an activity, or spending.
examples: Wartime rationing [[curtailed]] travel, so many families spent their summers close to home.

lookalikes.tell: Curtail means cut back; entail means involve as a necessary part.

meaning: Believing that people act mainly out of self-interest, and so distrusting their motives.
examples: After watching so many reform campaigns fade, the reporter had grown [[cynical]], assuming each new promise was just a bid for votes.
uses: In answer choices: "The narrator takes a cynical view of the politicians' promises."

meaning: To make someone feel afraid or discouraged, especially about facing a difficult task.
examples: The steep, icy walls of the gorge did not [[daunt]] the survey team, who spent a month mapping them.

lookalikes.tell: Daunt means discourage or intimidate; taunt means mock or tease.
Daunt means discourage; vaunt means boast about.

meaning: Seeming so hard or large that it discourages people from trying.
examples: Mapping every star in the galaxy seemed a [[daunting]] task, but the team broke it into manageable pieces.

lookalikes.tell: Daunting means intimidating; taunting means mocking.
Daunting means discouraging; dauntless means fearless.

meaning: A shortage or lack of something.
examples: The [[dearth]] of written records from the period forces historians to rely on archaeology.

lookalikes.tell: Dearth means shortage; death means the end of life.

meaning: To make someone or something very weak and less able to function.
examples: The fever [[debilitated]] the soldiers so badly that many could not stand, let alone march.
partners: a debilitating illness / debilitate an economy

lookalikes.tell: Debilitate means make weak; rehabilitate means restore to health or good condition.

meaning: To reach a conclusion by reasoning from facts or clues.
short: reason to a conclusion that must follow
examples: From the shape of its teeth, paleontologists [[deduced]] that the animal ate mostly hard seeds.

lookalikes.tell: Deduce means reason out; deduct means subtract.

meaning: To consider or judge something to be a certain way.
examples: The council [[deemed]] the old bridge unsafe and closed it to traffic.

lookalikes.tell: Deem means judge to be; doom means condemn to a bad fate.

meaning: Firmly established over a long time and hard to change.
examples: The festival reflects a [[deep-rooted]] tradition that villagers have kept alive for more than three centuries.

meaning: To give reasons for accepting or protecting a position.
examples: The author uses new records to [[defend]] her earlier conclusion.

lookalikes.tell: Defend supports a position; depend means rely on something.

uses: In answer choices: "The author defends the experiment's design against a common criticism."

meaning: Without any protection against attack or harm.
examples: Newly hatched sea turtles are almost [[defenseless]], and many are caught by birds before they reach the water.

lookalikes.tell: Defenseless means without protection; defensible means able to be justified or protected.

meaning: Quick to protect oneself against criticism, often by reacting too strongly.
examples: Asked about the missing funds, the treasurer grew [[defensive]] and refused to answer.
The author's [[defensive]] preface answers critics who had not yet reviewed the book.

lookalikes.tell: Defensive describes someone guarding against criticism; defensible describes a position that can be justified.

uses: In answer choices: "The scientist's reply is defensive, dismissing the criticism rather than addressing it."

meaning: To postpone an action or decision.
examples: The committee voted to [[defer]] its decision until more data arrived.

lookalikes.tell: Defer means postpone; differ means be unlike or disagree.

meaning: To give way to another person's opinion, judgment or authority, usually out of respect; used as “defer to.”
examples: On questions of navigation, the captain [[deferred]] to the old pilot, who had sailed the strait for forty years.
The court usually [[defers]] to Congress on matters of foreign trade.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The young king could have delayed the decision, but instead he [[deferred]] to his ministers, who urged him to make peace at once.
nearly.clue: to his ministers, who urged him to make peace at once

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Although she led the expedition, the geologist [[deferred]] to her guide on the route across the glacier, since he could read the ice in ways she could not.
nearly.clue: since he could read the ice in ways she could not

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Aunt Harriet had strong opinions about the ball, but in the end she [[deferred]] to her brother, as she did in all things, and the ball was held.
nearly.clue: as she did in all things, and the ball was held

lookalikes.tell: Defer means yield to someone or delay something; differ means be unlike or disagree.

meaning: Showing polite respect, often by yielding to someone else's judgment or wishes.
examples: The young clerk's letters to the senator are [[deferential]], full of apologies for taking up his time.

lookalikes.tell: Deferential means respectful; differential means relating to a difference.
Deferential means respectful; deferred means put off until later.

uses: In answer choices: "The letter's tone is deferential, as the writer repeatedly praises the governor's judgment."

meaning: Openly and boldly refusing to obey authority.
examples: Even after the court's ruling, the editor remained [[defiant]], printing the banned essay on the paper's front page.

lookalikes.tell: Defiant means openly resisting authority; deviant means departing from accepted norms.

meaning: Final and conclusive, settling a question with authority.
examples: Until the tomb's inscription was translated, historians had no [[definitive]] proof of the king's name.

lookalikes.tell: Definitive means final and authoritative, settling a question; definite simply means clear or certain.

meaning: Causing harm or damage, often in ways that are not obvious at first.
examples: The study found that even small amounts of the pesticide had [[deleterious]] effects on bees' ability to navigate.

lookalikes.tell: Deleterious means harmful; delirious means wildly confused or excited.

meaning: Planned or considered rather than accidental or hasty.
examples: The repeated phrase was a [[deliberate]] choice by the poet.

meaning: To outline or describe something in a precise way.
examples: The report [[delineates]] the roles of the two agencies.

lookalikes.tell: Delineate outlines clearly; delete removes text.

meaning: To make a point clear through evidence or example.
examples: The experiment [[demonstrates]] how salt affects freezing.
uses: In answer choices: "It demonstrates that the method works on a larger scale."

meaning: To indicate a particular meaning or thing.
examples: In the diagram, blue marks [[denote]] freshwater channels.

lookalikes.tell: Denote states direct meaning; connote suggests an association.

meaning: To portray a subject in an image or description.
examples: The mural [[depicts]] workers rebuilding the harbor.

lookalikes.tell: Depict portrays; predict says what may happen later.

uses: In answer choices: "The passage depicts the town as quiet and closed to outsiders."

meaning: To put resources, tools, or troops into position or use for a purpose.
examples: The city [[deployed]] extra snowplows along the main roads hours before the storm arrived.

lookalikes.tell: Deploy means put into use; deplore means strongly disapprove of.

meaning: To take something away from someone, or to keep them from having something they need or want.
short: take away or deny something needed
examples: The blockade [[deprived]] the city of grain for nearly two years.

lookalikes.tell: Deprive means take away; derive means obtain from a source.
Deprive means take away; depraved means morally corrupt.

meaning: To mock or ridicule someone or something as foolish or worthless.
examples: Critics [[derided]] the Impressionists' first exhibition, calling the paintings unfinished sketches.

lookalikes.tell: Deride means mock; derive means obtain from, or come from, a source.

uses: In answer choices: "The author derides the proposal as naive and poorly thought out."

meaning: Expressing mocking scorn; making fun of someone or something.
examples: The crowd greeted the inventor's flying machine with [[derisive]] laughter.
In a [[derisive]] review, the critic called the play “a long nap with costumes.”

lookalikes.tell: Derisive means mocking; derivative means copied from something else and unoriginal.

uses: In answer choices: "The author's tone is derisive, mocking the claims made in the company's advertisements."

meaning: To get or trace something from an earlier source or basis.
examples: The researchers [[derive]] their estimate from survey records.

lookalikes.tell: Derive gets from a source; deprive takes something away.

meaning: To tell what something is like by giving details about it, without necessarily judging or explaining it.
examples: The first paragraph [[describes]] the valley as it looked before the dam was built.
In her journal, the botanist [[described]] forty plants that European scientists had never recorded.
partners: describe a process / a scene / describe X as

lookalikes.tell: Describe means tell what something is like; prescribe means order a remedy or a rule.

uses: In answer choices: "The text describes a common method, then explains why it often fails."

meaning: To stop doing something, especially when asked or ordered to.
examples: The court ordered the company to [[desist]] from selling the device until its safety had been tested.

lookalikes.tell: Desist means stop doing something; resist means withstand or fight against.

meaning: Lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm; jumping from one thing to another.
examples: After months of [[desultory]] study, he finally made a schedule and worked through the textbook chapter by chapter.

lookalikes.tell: Desultory means aimless; dilatory means slow or delaying.
Desultory means aimless; sultry means hot and humid.

meaning: Not emotionally involved; standing apart and viewing things calmly or objectively.
examples: The narrator describes the battle in a [[detached]] voice, as if reporting the weather.

lookalikes.tell: Detached means emotionally distant; detailed means full of particulars.
Detached means standing apart emotionally; attached means fond of or connected to.

uses: In answer choices: "The narrator describes the events in a detached, almost clinical tone."

meaning: To discourage someone from doing something, usually by making them fear the results.
examples: Bright lights along the fence are meant to [[deter]] deer from entering the orchard.

lookalikes.tell: Deter discourages an action; defer postpones it.

meaning: To become gradually worse in condition or quality.
examples: Without regular care, the old manuscripts [[deteriorated]], their pages turning brittle and brown.

lookalikes.tell: Deteriorate means become worse; deter means discourage someone from acting.

meaning: Something that discourages people or animals from taking an action.
examples: Bright warning colors act as a [[deterrent]], signaling to birds that the frog tastes bitter and may be poisonous.
partners: a deterrent to / an effective deterrent

lookalikes.tell: A deterrent discourages an action; a detergent is a cleaning substance.

meaning: Tending to cause harm or damage.
examples: Too much fertilizer can be [[detrimental]] to nearby streams, where it feeds algae blooms.

lookalikes.tell: Detrimental means harmful; detritus means loose debris.

meaning: To move away from an expected course, rule, or standard.
examples: The ship's log shows that the captain [[deviated]] from the planned route to avoid a storm.

lookalikes.tell: Deviate means stray from a path; devise means invent a plan.

meaning: Using sneaky, indirect, and dishonest methods to get what one wants.
examples: In the novel, the [[devious]] steward forges letters to turn the two brothers against each other.

lookalikes.tell: Devious means sneaky and dishonest; divisive means causing disagreement between people.

meaning: To spread out over a wide area or among many people. As an adjective, it means spread out and not concentrated.
examples: New farming techniques [[diffused]] slowly from village to village along the river valley.

lookalikes.tell: Diffuse means spread out; defuse means calm a tense situation or disarm a bomb.

meaning: Calm, serious, and self-respecting in manner.
examples: Despite the crowd's jeers, the elderly senator gave a [[dignified]] reply, speaking slowly and never raising her voice.

lookalikes.tell: Dignified describes a serious, composed manner; a dignitary is an important official.

meaning: To move away from the main subject for a while when speaking or writing.
examples: The essay [[digresses]] into a story about the author's grandfather before returning to its argument about farm policy.

lookalikes.tell: Digress means wander off the topic; regress means go back to an earlier, often worse, state.
Digress means stray from the point; digest means absorb food or information.

uses: In answer choices: "The author digresses to describe her own first visit to the site."

meaning: A temporary departure from the main subject in speech or writing.
short: a turn away from the main topic
examples: After a long [[digression]] about his grandfather's farm, the speaker finally returned to the subject of water policy.
partners: a brief digression / a digression from

lookalikes.tell: A digression wanders from the main topic; a regression moves back to an earlier state.

uses: In answer choices: "The second paragraph is a brief digression about the author's childhood."

meaning: Slow to act, or meant to cause delay.
examples: The committee's [[dilatory]] approach meant its report arrived a year after the problem had worsened.

lookalikes.tell: Dilatory means slow to act; dilated means widened.
Dilatory means delaying; desultory means aimless.

meaning: Hardworking and careful in doing a task.
examples: A [[diligent]] observer, she recorded the temperature of the pond every morning for eleven years.

lookalikes.tell: Diligent means careful and hardworking; a dilettante dabbles in a subject without serious effort.

meaning: To reduce in size, importance, or strength.
examples: The effect began to [[diminish]] after the first week.
partners: diminish over time / the value of

lookalikes.tell: Diminish lessens; demolish destroys completely.

meaning: To deny any responsibility for, connection with, or support of something.
examples: When the letter became public, the party quickly [[disavowed]] it, insisting that no official had approved its contents.
partners: disavow a statement / disavow any role

lookalikes.tell: Disavow means deny any link to; avow means declare openly.

uses: In answer choices: "The speaker disavows the views expressed in her earlier book."

meaning: To recognize something that is difficult to see or understand.
examples: The team could [[discern]] a pattern in the noisy data.

lookalikes.tell: Discern notices a subtle pattern; disregard chooses to ignore it.

meaning: To reveal information that was previously hidden.
examples: The author did not [[disclose]] the source of the letters.

lookalikes.tell: Disclose reveals information; enclose surrounds or contains it.

meaning: To stop doing, making, or providing something.
examples: The company [[discontinued]] the model after tests revealed a flaw in its brakes.
partners: discontinue a product / a service / treatment

lookalikes.tell: Discontinue means stop; discontent means dissatisfaction.
Discontinue means stop; discontinuous means having gaps or breaks.

meaning: Not in agreement or harmony; clashing, whether in opinions, findings, or sounds.
examples: The two surveys produced [[discordant]] results, one showing the lake's fish population rising and the other showing it falling.

lookalikes.tell: Discordant means clashing or disagreeing; disconcerting means unsettling.

meaning: To treat an idea, a claim or a possibility as unimportant or unlikely to be true.
examples: Investigators could not [[discount]] the possibility that the fire was set on purpose.
Early critics [[discounted]] her findings because she lacked a university post.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Merchants who had cut their prices to draw customers [[discounted]] the rumors of war, and many were ruined when the ports closed.
nearly.clue: and many were ruined when the ports closed

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: At first, the team [[discounted]] the strange reading as a fault in the equipment, but it appeared again on three different instruments.
nearly.clue: as a fault in the equipment

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Martha [[discounted]] her sister's warnings about the new tenant, and she regretted it the day he left without paying.
nearly.clue: and she regretted it the day he left without paying

partners: discount a possibility / a claim / a warning

lookalikes.tell: Discount a claim means give it little weight yourself; discredit a claim means make others doubt it.

meaning: To try to stop someone from doing something, or to make an action less likely.
examples: High freight fees [[discouraged]] many farmers from shipping their grain by rail.

lookalikes.tell: Discourage means deter; disparage means belittle.

meaning: To make a claim, idea, or person seem false or untrustworthy.
examples: Later excavations [[discredited]] the theory that the city had been abandoned after a flood.
partners: discredit a theory / a witness / a rival

lookalikes.tell: Discredit means damage trust in; discreet means careful not to attract attention.

uses: In answer choices: "The second paragraph discredits an earlier explanation by showing that its key data were misread."

meaning: A mismatch between results, accounts, or expectations.
examples: The two dates show a [[discrepancy]] the historian cannot yet explain.

lookalikes.tell: Discrepancy is a mismatch; discretion is careful judgment.

meaning: Able to judge quality well and to notice fine differences, as in “a discriminating reader.”
examples: A [[discriminating]] collector, she bought only a few paintings, but each was a masterpiece.
The shop is aimed at [[discriminating]] buyers willing to pay for handmade work.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Unlike the other patrons at court, who bought whatever was fashionable, the duchess was a [[discriminating]] buyer of art, rejecting nine paintings for every one she kept.
nearly.clue: rejecting nine paintings for every one she kept

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Honeybees are [[discriminating]] foragers: they can tell apart flowers whose nectar differs in sugar by only a few percent, and they favor the sweeter ones.
nearly.clue: they can tell apart flowers whose nectar differs in sugar by only a few percent

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The editor had a [[discriminating]] ear; she could hear at once which line in a poem was false, and she cut it without mercy.
nearly.clue: she could hear at once which line in a poem was false

lookalikes.tell: Discriminating means able to judge quality; discriminatory means treating people unfairly.

meaning: Showing that one considers someone or something unworthy of respect or attention.
examples: The academy's senior members were [[disdainful]] of painters who worked outdoors.
She gave the cheap souvenir a [[disdainful]] glance and walked on.

lookalikes.tell: Disdainful describes a person showing scorn; distasteful describes something unpleasant or offensive.

uses: In answer choices: "The narrator is disdainful of the town's fashionable society."

meaning: Unwilling or not wanting to do something.
examples: Tired after the long voyage, the crew were [[disinclined]] to explore the island until morning.

lookalikes.tell: Disinclined means unwilling; declined means refused, or went down.

meaning: Not sincere or candid, especially by pretending to know less, or to be more honest, than one really is.
examples: Critics called the company's claim that it had never studied the risks [[disingenuous]], since its own scientists had warned of them for years.

lookalikes.tell: Ingenuous means innocent and trusting; disingenuous means only pretending to be.
Disingenuous means insincere; ingenious means clever and inventive.

uses: In answer choices: "The author suggests that the official's surprise at the report was disingenuous."

meaning: Not influenced by any personal gain; impartial. It does not mean uninterested.
examples: The dispute was finally settled by a [[disinterested]] panel whose members owned no land along the river.

lookalikes.tell: Disinterested means impartial, with nothing to gain; uninterested means bored or not curious.

meaning: Gloomy and depressing; also, very poor in quality or result.
examples: After a [[dismal]] potato harvest in 1846, tens of thousands of families left Ireland for North America.

lookalikes.tell: Dismal means gloomy; a dismissal is a sending away or firing.
Dismal describes something gloomy; dismayed describes a person upset by something unexpected.

meaning: To set aside a claim or concern without accepting it.
examples: The reviewer [[dismisses]] the objection as irrelevant.

lookalikes.tell: Dismiss rejects a point; disperse scatters things.

uses: In answer choices: "The author dismisses the objection as based on a misunderstanding."

meaning: Showing that one thinks something is not worth considering.
examples: Early reviewers were [[dismissive]] of the novel, calling it a minor book about unimportant people.

lookalikes.tell: Dismissive describes an attitude; a dismissal is the act of sending someone away.

uses: In answer choices: "The critic is dismissive of the novel, treating it as unworthy of serious attention."

meaning: Lacking order or discipline; unruly or messy.
examples: Guards arrested several men for [[disorderly]] conduct after the crowd outside the courthouse began throwing stones.

lookalikes.tell: Disorderly usually describes unruly behavior; disordered describes something thrown out of its normal arrangement or working.

meaning: Poorly planned or arranged, so that it works badly.
examples: The early experiments were so [[disorganized]] that no one could tell which plots had received the new fertilizer.

lookalikes.tell: Disorganized means poorly arranged; disoriented means confused about where one is.

meaning: To speak of someone or something as unimportant or of little worth.
examples: Critics at first [[disparaged]] the painter's loose brushwork as sloppy, but within a decade museums were competing to buy her canvases.

lookalikes.tell: Disparage means belittle; disparate means fundamentally different.

uses: In answer choices: "The author disparages the earlier studies as small and careless."

meaning: So different in kind that they are hard to compare or combine.
examples: The exhibit brings together [[disparate]] objects, from Roman coins to space-age tools, to tell a single story about trade.

lookalikes.tell: Disparate means very different; desperate means hopeless or willing to try anything.

meaning: A large difference between two or more things, often one that seems unfair.
examples: The survey revealed a wide [[disparity]] between rural and urban access to clinics.
partners: a disparity between / in income / in wealth

lookalikes.tell: Disparity is a gap; disparage means belittle.

meaning: Not influenced by strong emotion, and so able to judge calmly and fairly.
examples: Even when describing the devastating flood, the report stayed [[dispassionate]], listing losses and causes without a single emotional word.

lookalikes.tell: Dispassionate means free of emotion; compassionate means feeling sympathy for others.

uses: In answer choices: "The author keeps a dispassionate tone while describing the disaster."

meaning: Speed and efficiency in getting something done; usually used as “with dispatch.”
examples: The clerk handled every request with [[dispatch]], and the line never grew long.
The repairs were finished with a [[dispatch]] that surprised the whole town.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The general's riders carried his orders with such [[dispatch]] that his officers often received them before the enemy had moved.
nearly.clue: that his officers often received them before the enemy had moved

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Once the leak was found, the engineers acted with [[dispatch]], sealing the pipe within an hour.
nearly.clue: sealing the pipe within an hour

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Mrs. Hale packed the trunks and posted the letters with her usual [[dispatch]], and the family was on the road by noon.
nearly.clue: and the family was on the road by noon

meaning: To make a doubt, fear, or false belief go away.
short: drive away a belief or fear
examples: The new data helped [[dispel]] the myth that sharks must keep swimming to survive.

lookalikes.tell: Dispel drives away a belief or fear; dispense gives something out.

meaning: Not necessary; able to be done without.
short: not needed; can be done without
examples: Once the canal opened, the old wagon road seemed [[dispensable]], and the county stopped repairing it.

lookalikes.tell: Dispensable means not needed; to dispense is to hand out.
Dispensable means can be done without; indispensable means absolutely necessary.

meaning: To argue that a claim is untrue or wrong.
examples: Several scientists [[dispute]] the estimate, arguing that the survey missed animals living in caves.

lookalikes.tell: Dispute means argue against; disrepute means a bad reputation.

uses: In answer choices: "It disputes the claim that the drought caused the city's decline."

meaning: To pay no attention to something, often deliberately.
examples: The report [[disregards]] the concerns of farmers, focusing only on the effects in cities.

lookalikes.tell: Disregard means ignore; regard means consider or look at.

meaning: To interrupt or disturb the normal course of an activity or process.
examples: Road construction [[disrupted]] the birds' nesting season, and fewer chicks hatched that year.

lookalikes.tell: Disrupt throws something into disorder; erupt bursts out.

meaning: To spread information, ideas, or knowledge widely.
examples: Printers in Philadelphia [[disseminated]] the pamphlet so quickly that it reached every colony within weeks.

lookalikes.tell: Disseminate means spread widely; dissemble means hide one's true feelings or motives.

meaning: To hold or express disagreement with an official or widely held view.
examples: Two of the nine justices [[dissented]], arguing in a sharply worded opinion that the law violated the right to free speech.

lookalikes.tell: Dissent is disagreement; descent is a movement downward, or a person's ancestry.

meaning: To scatter and fade away gradually until gone, as fog, heat, or tension does. It can also mean to waste money or energy foolishly.
examples: By midmorning the fog had [[dissipated]], revealing the ridge the hikers had been aiming for.
partners: tension / fog / heat dissipates; dissipate energy

lookalikes.tell: Dissipate means scatter until gone; disseminate means spread information widely on purpose.

meaning: To persuade someone not to do or believe something.
examples: Her friends tried to [[dissuade]] her from sailing alone across the Atlantic, but she had already stocked the boat.

lookalikes.tell: Dissuade means talk someone out of something; persuade means talk them into it.

meaning: Recognizably different from something else.
examples: The survey found two [[distinct]] patterns of migration.

lookalikes.tell: Distinct means clearly different; discreet means tactful or private.

meaning: To change the shape or meaning of something inaccurately.
examples: The graph's truncated axis can [[distort]] the trend.

lookalikes.tell: Distort changes a picture misleadingly; disclose reveals hidden information.

meaning: So upset or worried that one cannot think clearly.
examples: [[Distraught]] after the fire destroyed her notes, the botanist spent the next year retracing her route to collect new samples.

lookalikes.tell: Distraught means deeply upset; distract means draw attention away.
Distraught describes an upset person; fraught means full of something, usually tension or risk.

meaning: Moving apart or differing from one another, as opinions, paths, or results can.
examples: The two populations of finches, separated for thousands of years, developed [[divergent]] beak shapes.

lookalikes.tell: Divergent means moving apart from one another; diverse means varied, made up of many kinds.

meaning: Made up of many different types or perspectives.
examples: The archive holds a [[diverse]] range of personal accounts.

lookalikes.tell: Diverse means varied; divergent means moving or thinking apart.

meaning: To take something, such as power or property, away from someone, or to get rid of something one owns.
short: strip of, or get rid of
examples: The new constitution [[divested]] the monarch of most of his powers, leaving him a largely ceremonial role.

lookalikes.tell: Divest means strip away or sell off; invest means put money or effort in.

meaning: Causing strong disagreement or hostility between people.
examples: The question of tariffs proved so [[divisive]] that the party split into two factions.

lookalikes.tell: Divisive means causing disagreement; decisive means settling something firmly.
Divisive means splitting people apart; derisive means mocking.

meaning: To make known something private or secret.
examples: The reporter refused to [[divulge]] the names of the officials who had given her the documents.

lookalikes.tell: Divulge means reveal; diverge means move apart.
Divulge means reveal a secret; indulge means allow oneself a pleasure.

meaning: Quiet and easily controlled, led, or taught.
examples: Unlike their wild ancestors, the [[docile]] farm foxes let visitors pet them and even wagged their tails.

lookalikes.tell: Docile means easily managed; a docent is a guide in a museum.

meaning: To provide a record that supports the existence of something.
examples: The photographs [[document]] changes to the shoreline.

lookalikes.tell: Document records evidence; doctrine is a body of beliefs.

meaning: Stating opinions as if they were certainly true, and refusing to consider other views or evidence.
short: rigidly insisting one's views are right
examples: The young astronomer found her [[dogmatic]] professor unwilling even to look at the new measurements.

lookalikes.tell: Dogmatic means rigidly sure of one's beliefs; pragmatic means focused on what works in practice.
Dogmatic means unbending in opinion; dramatic means striking or theatrical.

uses: In answer choices: "The critic's tone is dogmatic, allowing no room for other readings of the poem."

meaning: Exerting the greatest influence or appearing most often.
short: having the most power or influence
examples: One species became [[dominant]] in the restored habitat.

lookalikes.tell: Dominant means most influential; domineering means overcontrolling.

meaning: To make something seem less important or serious than it is.
examples: Early reports [[downplayed]] the epidemic, calling it a seasonal fever that would pass by winter.
uses: In answer choices: "The author downplays the significance of the earlier study's findings."

meaning: Extremely harsh and severe, especially of laws or punishments.
examples: Under the [[draconian]] new code, stealing a loaf of bread could be punished with years in prison.

meaning: Extreme and far-reaching in effect, often taken suddenly.
