partners: grounds for concern / on the grounds that

lookalikes.tell: Grounds are reasons for a belief; grounded means sensible and realistic, or kept from going out.

meaning: Introducing new ideas or methods for the first time; pioneering.
examples: Her [[groundbreaking]] study was the first to show that trees share nutrients through underground networks of fungi.

meaning: Given or done unwillingly, as in “grudging respect” or “a grudging admission.”
examples: The rival coach offered [[grudging]] praise for the team's defense.
Over time, the townspeople developed a [[grudging]] respect for the stubborn newcomer.

lookalikes.tell: Grudging means given unwillingly; grueling means exhausting.

uses: In answer choices: "The critic offers grudging admiration for a novel she otherwise dislikes."

meaning: Extremely tiring and demanding.
examples: After a [[grueling]] twelve-hour climb through snow and wind, the team finally reached the summit.

lookalikes.tell: Grueling means exhausting; gruesome means horrifying and repulsive.

meaning: To promise or arrange that a result will occur.
short: formally promise that it will happen
examples: The contract cannot [[guarantee]] that supplies will arrive early.

meaning: Innocent and sincere, without any wish or ability to deceive.
examples: The child's [[guileless]] questions, asked without a hint of mockery, made the stern old judge laugh for the first time in weeks.

lookalikes.tell: Guileless means free of deceit; guiltless means free of blame.

meaning: A tendency to believe things too easily, which makes a person easy to trick.
examples: The 1835 hoax, a newspaper report of bat-winged people living on the moon, played on readers' [[gullibility]].

lookalikes.tell: Gullibility is being easily fooled; guile is cunning used to fool others.
Gullibility means being easily tricked; culpability means being to blame.

meaning: Easily fooled into believing things that are not true.
examples: The swindler sold shares in a gold mine that did not exist to [[gullible]] investors who never asked to see it.

lookalikes.tell: Gullible means easily fooled; guileless means unwilling or unable to fool others.

meaning: Used so often that it has become dull and has lost its original force.
examples: The speech was full of [[hackneyed]] phrases like "at the end of the day" and "think outside the box."

lookalikes.tell: A hack is a writer who churns out dull work; hackneyed describes the stale phrases such writing is full of.

meaning: To praise someone or something publicly and enthusiastically; often used as “hailed as.”
everyday: call out to, as to stop a taxi
examples: Critics [[hailed]] the novel as the finest of the decade.
The treaty was [[hailed]] as a turning point in relations between the two nations.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: When the battered ship sailed back into the harbor, crowds lined the docks to [[hail]] its crew as heroes of the voyage.
nearly.clue: as heroes of the voyage

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Doctors [[hailed]] the vaccine as a triumph, since it cut cases of the disease by ninety percent in its first year.
nearly.clue: as a triumph

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The villagers, who had once mocked the young poet, now [[hailed]] her as their greatest daughter.
nearly.clue: who had once mocked the young poet

lookalikes.tell: Hail means praise publicly; hale means healthy and strong.

meaning: To slow down or get in the way of progress or movement.
examples: Heavy fog [[hampered]] the search, forcing the boats to return to shore.

lookalikes.tell: Hamper hinders; pamper indulges with care.

meaning: Lacking any plan, order, or direction; done at random.
examples: The early collections were stored in a [[haphazard]] way, with fossils and pottery shards crammed into the same drawers.

lookalikes.tell: Haphazard means random and unplanned; hazardous means dangerous.

meaning: A person or thing that signals that something is about to happen.
short: a sign of what is coming
examples: The first robins are a [[harbinger]] of spring in the northern states, arriving just as the ground begins to thaw.

lookalikes.tell: A harbinger announces what is coming; a harbor is a sheltered place for ships.

meaning: To keep a thought or feeling, such as a doubt, a hope or a grudge, in one's mind, often secretly and for a long time.
examples: Some members of the committee [[harbored]] doubts about the plan but kept silent.
For years she [[harbored]] the hope of returning to her village.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The captain welcomed the rival fleet into port with every courtesy, though he privately [[harbored]] the suspicion that its commander was a spy.
nearly.clue: the suspicion that its commander was a spy

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Although he published the standard account of the disease, the doctor [[harbored]] doubts about it, which he confessed only in letters to his brother.
nearly.clue: which he confessed only in letters to his brother

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Though she smiled at her cousin across the table, Maud still [[harbored]] a grudge over the ruined dress, and she meant to settle it.
nearly.clue: a grudge over the ruined dress

partners: harbor doubts / suspicions / a grudge / hopes

lookalikes.tell: Harbor a doubt means hold it in mind; a harbinger is a sign of something to come.

meaning: Strong enough to survive difficult conditions.
examples: Only a few [[hardy]] shrubs grow on the ridge, where winter winds strip away the snow.

lookalikes.tell: Hardy means tough; hearty means warm and enthusiastic, or large and filling.
Hardy means tough; tardy means late.

meaning: Consistent and pleasing because its parts work well together.
examples: The composer made a [[harmonious]] blend of two musical traditions.

lookalikes.tell: Harmonious describes pleasing agreement; harmonic relates to musical tones.

meaning: To control and make use of something, especially a natural force or resource.
examples: Mills along the river [[harnessed]] its current to grind grain and, later, to spin cotton.

lookalikes.tell: Harness means put to use; harass means repeatedly bother.

meaning: To make something happen sooner or faster; also, to move or act quickly.
examples: The drought [[hastened]] the decline of the city, which had already been losing trade to its rivals.

lookalikes.tell: Hasten is the verb (speed up); haste is the noun (hurry).
Hasten means speed up; chasten means humble or correct someone.

meaning: Behaving as if one is better or more important than other people; arrogantly proud.
examples: The [[haughty]] duchess refused to speak to anyone who had not been properly introduced.

lookalikes.tell: Haughty means proud and scornful; naughty means badly behaved.
Haughty means arrogant; hardy means tough and able to endure.

meaning: To pay careful attention to advice or a warning and act on it.
examples: Had the town [[heeded]] the geologists' warnings, it might have moved its school away from the fault line.
partners: heed a warning / advice / a call

lookalikes.tell: Heed means pay attention to; heel means the back of the foot, or to follow closely.

meaning: Leadership or dominance, especially of one country or group over others.
examples: For most of the nineteenth century, Britain's naval [[hegemony]] allowed it to protect trade routes around the world.

lookalikes.tell: Hegemony is dominance; homogeneity is sameness throughout.

meaning: Reluctant to act or speak because of doubt.
examples: The committee was [[hesitant]] to accept the untested method.

meaning: Made up of parts or members that are different from one another.
examples: The soil samples were [[heterogeneous]], mixing clay, sand, and volcanic ash within a single layer.

lookalikes.tell: Heterogeneous means made of different parts; homogeneous means the same throughout.

meaning: To make a feature or point especially noticeable.
examples: The author uses the comparison to [[highlight]] a key difference.
partners: highlight a problem / the role of
uses: In answer choices: "It highlights a contrast between the two characters' reactions."

meaning: To slow or obstruct a process without necessarily stopping it.
examples: The missing records may [[hinder]] the investigation.

meaning: To believe or state that something is true; used as “hold that.” A court that holds something rules it.
examples: Many economists [[hold]] that small tax cuts have little effect on hiring.
The court [[held]] that the law violated the right to free speech.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The treaty's defenders, waving copies of it at the rally, [[held]] that it would end the border raids for good.
nearly.clue: that it would end the border raids for good

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: For centuries, most naturalists [[held]] that species never changed; fossils of creatures no longer living slowly forced them to think again.
nearly.clue: that species never changed

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Grandfather, gripping his cane, [[held]] that no honest man had ever made money at cards, and he would hear no argument on the point.
nearly.clue: and he would hear no argument on the point

lookalikes.tell: Hold that means maintain as true; behold means see or look at.

uses: In answer choices: "Some scientists hold that the decline is only temporary."

meaning: Treating something as a whole, with attention to how its parts connect, rather than one part at a time.
examples: Instead of treating each symptom separately, the clinic takes a [[holistic]] approach, looking at the patient's diet, sleep, and stress together.

lookalikes.tell: Holistic means considering the whole system; wholesale means done on a large scale without distinction.

meaning: The same in kind or makeup throughout.
examples: Early settlers described the prairie as a [[homogeneous]] sea of grass, but botanists later counted hundreds of species there.

lookalikes.tell: Homogeneous means the same throughout; heterogeneous means made of different parts.

meaning: Showing active opposition or antagonism.
examples: The proposal faced a [[hostile]] response from residents.

lookalikes.tell: Hostile is unfriendly; hospitable welcomes guests.

meaning: Excessive pride or self-confidence, especially the kind that leads to a downfall.
examples: Historians often blame the general's [[hubris]] for the defeat: sure that no army would cross the river, he never sent scouts to watch it.
partners: an act of hubris / the hubris of

lookalikes.tell: Hubris is excessive pride; a hubbub is a noisy commotion.

meaning: Showing compassion and trying to avoid causing pain or suffering.
examples: Reformers pushed for more [[humane]] prisons, with clean cells, decent food, and no chains.

lookalikes.tell: Humane means compassionate; human means relating to people.

meaning: Not claiming more importance or ability than one has.
examples: The scientist remained [[humble]] despite the award.

lookalikes.tell: Humble is modest; humiliate means make someone feel ashamed.

meaning: Funny, or meant to make people laugh.
examples: Twain's [[humorous]] story about a jumping frog first made him famous.
The letter's [[humorous]] tone hides a serious complaint about the rent.

lookalikes.tell: Humorous means funny; the humerus is the bone of the upper arm.

uses: In answer choices: "The anecdote is humorous, but it makes a serious point about the costs of haste."

meaning: To use resources such as money, food or strength carefully, so that they last.
examples: The explorers [[husbanded]] their food, eating half rations for the last month.
The runner [[husbanded]] her strength for the final lap.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: With her husband away at war, Mrs. Hale ran the farm alone and [[husbanded]] every coin, so that the family still had money when he returned.
nearly.clue: so that the family still had money when he returned

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Desert tortoises [[husband]] water with remarkable efficiency, storing it in their bladders for months during the dry season.
nearly.clue: storing it in their bladders for months

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Knowing the candles would have to last the winter, the old woman [[husbanded]] them, lighting only one each evening.
nearly.clue: lighting only one each evening

lookalikes.tell: Husband resources means use them sparingly; husbandry is the care of crops and farm animals.

meaning: Combining elements from two distinct sources or types.
examples: The artist created a [[hybrid]] form of sculpture and performance.

meaning: Deliberate exaggeration used for effect and not meant to be taken literally.
examples: When the author says the line at the post office stretched to the moon, she is using [[hyperbole]], not reporting a measurement.

lookalikes.tell: Hyperbole is exaggeration in language; a hyperbola is a curve in mathematics.

uses: In answer choices: "The author uses hyperbole to emphasize how crowded the city had become."

meaning: Claiming to hold beliefs or standards that one's own behavior does not follow.
examples: Critics called the senator [[hypocritical]] for denouncing wasteful spending while flying to every meeting by private jet.

lookalikes.tell: Hypocritical means not practicing what one preaches; hypercritical means too quick to find fault.
Hypocritical means insincere; hypothetical means imagined for the sake of argument.

meaning: A proposed explanation that can be examined against evidence.
examples: The team tested the [[hypothesis]] with a second data set.
partners: test a hypothesis / support a hypothesis

lookalikes.tell: A hypothesis is a testable explanation; hyperbole is exaggeration.

meaning: To propose an explanation that can be tested but has not yet been shown to be true.
examples: The team [[hypothesized]] that the birds use the earth's magnetic field to find their way.
Some historians [[hypothesize]] that the city was abandoned after its river changed course.

lookalikes.tell: Hypothesize means propose an explanation; synthesize means combine parts into a whole.

uses: In answer choices: "The researchers hypothesize that the decline was caused by warmer winters."

meaning: Imagined or proposed for the sake of argument or testing, rather than known to be real.
examples: To test the policy, the economists modeled a [[hypothetical]] town of ten thousand households.

lookalikes.tell: Hypothetical means imagined for argument; hypocritical means insincere.
Hypothetical is the adjective; a hypothesis is a proposed explanation to be tested.

uses: In answer choices: "It presents a hypothetical scenario to illustrate the principle described earlier."

meaning: Guided by high ideals, often more than by what is realistic.
examples: The [[idealistic]] young founders believed their newspaper could end corruption in the city within a year.

lookalikes.tell: Idealistic describes a person driven by high ideals; idealized describes something pictured as better than it really is.

uses: In answer choices: "The narrator now sees her younger self as idealistic, even naive."

meaning: To determine and state what something is.
examples: The researchers [[identify]] three previously unrecorded species.

lookalikes.tell: Identify is the act of naming; identity is what something is.

meaning: Peculiar to one person or thing; highly individual and unusual.
examples: Dickinson's [[idiosyncratic]] use of dashes puzzled her first editors, who removed most of them.

lookalikes.tell: Idiosyncratic means peculiar to one person; idiomatic means natural to a language's usual expressions.

meaning: Not allowed by law or by accepted rules of behavior.
examples: The treaty aimed to shut down the [[illicit]] trade in ivory that was driving elephants toward extinction.

lookalikes.tell: Illicit means illegal; elicit means draw out a response.
Illicit means forbidden; explicit means clearly stated.

meaning: To help explain or reveal the meaning of something.
examples: The letters [[illuminate]] the artist's early motives.

lookalikes.tell: Illuminate makes clear; eliminate removes.

meaning: Seeming real but not actually real; based on an illusion.
examples: The town's boom proved [[illusory]]: once the mine closed, the new shops and jobs disappeared within a year.
partners: illusory gains / an illusory sense of safety

lookalikes.tell: Illusory means not real; elusive means real but hard to find or grasp.

meaning: To explain or support a point with an example or image.
examples: The case study [[illustrates]] the broader pattern.

lookalikes.tell: Illustrate provides an example; allude refers indirectly.

uses: In answer choices: "It illustrates the general claim with a specific case."

meaning: Well known and greatly admired for past achievements.
examples: Over an [[illustrious]] career, the physicist won two major prizes and trained dozens of future leaders in the field.

lookalikes.tell: Illustrious means famous and admired; illustrative means serving as an example.

meaning: Not relevant or important to the matter at hand.
examples: Whether the letter was written in May or June is [[immaterial]]; what matters is that it was sent before the vote.

lookalikes.tell: Immaterial means not relevant; material, in an argument, means relevant and significant.

meaning: Extremely large in size, amount, or degree.
examples: The telescope's mirror is [[immense]], nearly eight meters across, so that it can gather light from the faintest galaxies.

lookalikes.tell: Immense means huge; immerse means plunge into, or absorb deeply.

meaning: Going beyond reasonable or proper limits.
examples: The doctor warned that [[immoderate]] use of the tonic could damage the liver.

lookalikes.tell: Immoderate means excessive; immodest means boastful or improper.

meaning: Unable to change or be changed; fixed forever.
examples: Early naturalists treated species as [[immutable]], each fixed in the form in which it was created.

lookalikes.tell: Immutable means unchangeable; immune means protected from disease or harm.

meaning: Fair because no side or person receives undue preference.
examples: To settle the dispute, both towns agreed to accept the ruling of an [[impartial]] judge from outside the region.

lookalikes.tell: Impartial means unbiased; partial means biased or incomplete.

meaning: Filled with or showing strong feeling, as in “an impassioned plea.”
examples: In 1852, Frederick Douglass gave an [[impassioned]] speech on what the Fourth of July meant to enslaved people.
In an [[impassioned]] letter, the scientist begged the council to protect the marsh.

lookalikes.tell: Impassioned means full of strong feeling; impassive means showing no feeling at all.

uses: In answer choices: "The speaker makes an impassioned appeal for the preservation of the forest."

meaning: Without any flaw or fault; perfect.
examples: Her [[impeccable]] records allowed later researchers to repeat every step of the experiment.

lookalikes.tell: Impeccable means flawless; impeachable means able to be charged with misconduct.

meaning: To delay or block the progress of something.
examples: Fallen trees [[impeded]] the flow of the stream, creating a chain of small ponds.

lookalikes.tell: Impede slows something down; impel pushes it forward.

meaning: So slight or gradual that it cannot be noticed.
examples: The glacier's movement is [[imperceptible]] from one day to the next, but over a century it has retreated two miles.

lookalikes.tell: Imperceptible means unnoticeable; impervious means not affected by something, or not letting it through.
Imperceptible describes a change too slight to notice; perceptive describes a person who notices a lot.

meaning: To put someone or something in danger.
examples: Rising water temperatures [[imperil]] the reef, since corals bleach and die when the sea grows too warm.

lookalikes.tell: Imperil means put in danger; impair means weaken or damage.

meaning: Unable to be penetrated or affected by something (impervious to).
examples: The new coating makes the wood [[impervious]] to water, so the deck will not rot even after years of rain.

lookalikes.tell: Impervious means unaffected by something; imperious means arrogantly commanding.

meaning: Acting or done quickly and without thought or care.
examples: The [[impetuous]] young lieutenant charged the ridge before the rest of the regiment had arrived.

lookalikes.tell: Impetuous means rash; an impetus is a driving force.
Impetuous means hasty; impervious means unaffected by something or not letting it through.

meaning: A force or reason that makes something happen, or happen faster.
examples: The 1957 launch of Sputnik gave new [[impetus]] to science education in American schools.
partners: give impetus to; the impetus for / behind

lookalikes.tell: An impetus is a driving force; impetuous means rash.
An impetus pushes things forward; an impasse is a deadlock where no progress is possible.

meaning: Not seeming reasonable or likely to be true.
examples: Geologists found the claim that one flood had carved the canyon [[implausible]], since its rock showed millions of years of layered erosion.

lookalikes.tell: Implausible means hard to believe; impossible means it cannot happen at all.

meaning: To put a plan, decision, or agreement into effect.
examples: The city [[implemented]] the new recycling plan in stages, starting with the largest apartment buildings.

lookalikes.tell: Implement carries out a plan; implicate connects someone to wrongdoing.

meaning: Present in the meaning without being directly expressed.
examples: The warning is [[implicit]] in the final paragraph.

lookalikes.tell: Implicit is unstated; implicate links someone to an action.

meaning: To communicate a meaning indirectly.
examples: The phrase [[implies]] that the result was unexpected.
uses: In answer choices: "The author implies that the results may not apply to other regions."

meaning: To require someone to accept a rule, burden, or condition.
examples: The law would [[impose]] new reporting duties on firms.

lookalikes.tell: Impose places a burden on someone; expose reveals or subjects someone to risk.

meaning: Not sensible or workable in real conditions.
examples: The plan to heat the town with volcanic steam was clever but [[impractical]], since the nearest vents were forty miles away.

lookalikes.tell: Impractical means not sensible to do; impracticable means actually impossible to carry out.

meaning: Acting suddenly on a feeling or urge, without thinking first.
examples: Her [[impulsive]] decision to board the first ship to Lisbon changed the course of her career.

lookalikes.tell: Impulsive means acting on a sudden urge; compulsive means driven by an urge one cannot resist.

meaning: Not intended; happening by accident, often through carelessness.
examples: The discovery was [[inadvertent]]: the chemist had left a dish uncovered over the weekend and returned to find a strange mold growing in it.

lookalikes.tell: Inadvertent describes an accidental act; inattentive describes a person who is not paying attention.

meaning: Not relevant to a particular case, or not able to be used in it.
examples: The researchers argued that findings from laboratory mice were [[inapplicable]] to wild populations, which face very different food supplies.

lookalikes.tell: Inapplicable describes a rule or finding that does not apply; incapable describes someone unable to do something.

meaning: Something that encourages a particular action.
examples: The tax credit provides an [[incentive]] to preserve old buildings.

lookalikes.tell: An incentive encourages action; an incident is an event.

meaning: Happening as a minor or accidental part of something more important.
examples: The discovery of the fossil was [[incidental]] to the survey, which was meant to map the river's course.

lookalikes.tell: Incidental means minor and alongside the main thing; accidental means happening by chance.

meaning: Beginning to happen or develop; in an early stage.
examples: Doctors can treat the disease easily if they catch it at an [[incipient]] stage.
partners: an incipient stage / crisis; incipient signs

lookalikes.tell: Incipient means just beginning; insipid means bland and dull.
Incipient means just starting; a recipient is someone who receives something.

meaning: To stir up violent or unlawful behavior, or strong feeling, in others.
short: stir people to act, often violently
examples: Authorities arrested the pamphlet's printer, charging that its fiery words were meant to [[incite]] a riot.

lookalikes.tell: Incite means stir up; insight means deep understanding.

meaning: Including everyone or everything, with no one or nothing left out; also, including the limits named, as in "Monday to Friday inclusive."
short: including all; leaving no one out
examples: The new charter was more [[inclusive]], extending voting rights to residents who did not own land.

lookalikes.tell: Inclusive means including all; conclusive means settling a question.

meaning: So different or opposed that two things cannot exist, work or be true together.
short: unable to coexist or both be true
examples: The new fossil dates were [[incompatible]] with the long-held view that the two species never lived at the same time.

lookalikes.tell: Incompatible means unable to go together; incomparable means so good or so different that nothing compares.

uses: In answer choices: "The new data are incompatible with the researchers' original hypothesis."

meaning: Lacking the skill or ability to do something properly.
examples: The inquiry found that the [[incompetent]] manager had ignored three warnings about the cracked boiler.

lookalikes.tell: Incompetent means lacking skill; incompatible means unable to work or exist together.

meaning: Not leading to a firm conclusion or settling a question.
examples: Because the two trials produced conflicting results, the researchers called the evidence [[inconclusive]] and asked for a larger study.

lookalikes.tell: Inconclusive means not settling a question; inclusive means including everyone or everything.

uses: In answer choices: "It suggests that the evidence for the hypothesis remains inconclusive."

meaning: Strangely out of place; not in keeping with its surroundings or with what is expected.
examples: The glass-and-steel tower looked [[incongruous]] among the village's thatched cottages and narrow cobbled lanes.

lookalikes.tell: Incongruous means strikingly out of place; inconspicuous means not attracting attention at all.

meaning: Not important or significant; having little or no effect.
examples: Although the error in the census seemed [[inconsequential]], it was enough to shift one county's seat in the state legislature.

lookalikes.tell: Inconsequential means unimportant; inconsistent means not staying the same, or not agreeing with something else.

meaning: Contradictory across statements, observations, or actions.
examples: The witness's dates were [[inconsistent]] with the record.

lookalikes.tell: Inconsistent fails to agree; inconsequential has little effect.

meaning: So clearly true that it cannot be denied or disputed.
examples: The fingerprint on the glass was [[incontrovertible]] evidence that the suspect had been in the room.

lookalikes.tell: Incontrovertible means beyond dispute; controversial means causing dispute.
Incontrovertible means undeniable; inconvertible means unable to be exchanged or changed into something else.

meaning: Unwilling or unable to believe something.
examples: The audience was [[incredulous]] when the magician's assistant reappeared at the back of the hall.
Scientists were at first [[incredulous]] at reports of fish living in the underground lake.

lookalikes.tell: Incredulous describes a person who doesn't believe; incredible describes something hard to believe.

uses: In answer choices: "The narrator is incredulous at her brother's claim to have seen the comet."

meaning: Happening in a series of small steps or additions rather than all at once.
examples: Rather than a single breakthrough, the gain in battery life came from [[incremental]] changes to the design of the electrodes.

lookalikes.tell: Incremental means happening in small steps; instrumental means playing a key part in making something happen.

meaning: Impossible to erase, remove, or forget.
examples: The famine left an [[indelible]] mark on the region's culture, shaping its songs and stories for generations.

lookalikes.tell: Indelible means impossible to erase; inedible means not fit to eat.

meaning: To serve as a sign or provide information about something.
examples: Tree rings [[indicate]] that the region suffered a long drought in the 1500s, since the rings from those years are unusually thin.

lookalikes.tell: Indicate points to a conclusion; dictate commands or determines it.

meaning: Having no particular interest or concern; not caring one way or the other.
examples: The narrator's father seems [[indifferent]] to her success, never once asking about the prize she has won.
uses: In answer choices: "The character is indifferent to the opinions of her neighbors."

meaning: So important that it cannot be done without.
examples: Local guides were [[indispensable]] to the expedition, since only they knew where the springs were.

lookalikes.tell: Indispensable means absolutely necessary; indisposed means slightly ill or unwilling.

meaning: To cause a state, reaction, or action.
examples: The treatment may [[induce]] a measurable change in the cells.

lookalikes.tell: Induce brings about an effect; deduce reaches a conclusion by reasoning.

meaning: Not producing the intended effect; lacking the force or skill to get things done.
short: failing to have the desired effect
examples: The committee's warnings proved [[ineffectual]]: the factories kept dumping waste into the river for another decade.

lookalikes.tell: Ineffectual means failing to work; ineffable means too great to be put into words.
Ineffectual means it does not work at all; inefficient means it works but wastes time or resources.

meaning: Lacking skill, or acting in a clumsy, ineffective way.
examples: The general's [[inept]] handling of supplies left his troops without boots in the middle of winter.

lookalikes.tell: Inept means clumsy; inert means not moving or not reacting.
Inept means unskilled; adept means highly skilled.

meaning: Not moving or acting; in chemistry, not reacting with other substances.
examples: Because argon is chemically [[inert]], archives use it to shield fragile documents from the oxygen that slowly damages them.

lookalikes.tell: Inert means inactive; inept means clumsy or lacking skill.
Inert means inactive; inherent means built into something's nature.

meaning: Unable to be avoided given the conditions.
examples: The delay was [[inevitable]] once the bridge closed.

lookalikes.tell: Inevitable cannot be avoided; ineffable is too great for words.

meaning: To reach a conclusion on the basis of clues rather than a direct statement.
examples: From the wear marks on the handle, the team [[infers]] that the tool was used every day.

meaning: To make feelings, a conflict or a situation more intense or violent.
examples: The editorial, meant to calm the dispute, only [[inflamed]] tensions between the mill owners and the workers.

lookalikes.tell: To inflame is to stir up anger or conflict; to inflate is to fill with air or to exaggerate the size of something.

meaning: To have an effect on a decision, event, or development.
examples: Temperature can [[influence]] the time needed for the reaction.

lookalikes.tell: Influence affects an outcome; inference is a conclusion from clues.

meaning: To shape or deeply influence something, giving it its character; often used of ideas, experience or art.
examples: Her years as a nurse [[informed]] every chapter of her novel.
Religious belief [[informed]] much of the music composed in that period.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Toni Morrison's childhood in Ohio [[informs]] her fiction: several of her novels are set in Ohio, the state where she grew up.
nearly.clue: several of her novels are set in Ohio

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Studies of how birds fly have [[informed]] the design of aircraft wings, including the upturned tips that reduce drag.
nearly.clue: including the upturned tips that reduce drag

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Architects' study of ancient Greek temples [[informed]] the design of many early American banks and courthouses, with their tall columns and triangular roofs.
nearly.clue: with their tall columns and triangular roofs

partners: experience informs a work / an approach

lookalikes.tell: Inform means shape or tell; infirm means physically weak, especially from age.

meaning: Not happening often; occurring only now and then.
examples: Because rain is [[infrequent]] in the Atacama Desert, some of its plants survive for years on coastal fog alone.

lookalikes.tell: Infrequent means not happening often; an unfrequented place is one that few people visit.

meaning: To break a law or agreement, or to intrude on someone's rights.
examples: Critics argued that the new surveillance program [[infringed]] on citizens' right to privacy.
partners: infringe on rights / infringe a patent

lookalikes.tell: Infringe means violate a law or right; impinge means have an effect on something, often by pressing on it.

meaning: Clever and original, especially in solving a problem.
examples: The farmers built an [[ingenious]] system of channels that carried melting snow to fields miles away.

lookalikes.tell: Ingenious means clever; ingenuous means innocent and trusting.

meaning: Innocent and trusting; open and sincere in a way that can seem naive.
examples: The young clerk's [[ingenuous]] account of the firm's dealings, offered without a hint of suspicion, gave the investigators exactly what they needed.

lookalikes.tell: Ingenuous means innocent and trusting; ingenious means clever and inventive.

meaning: Existing as a natural, permanent part of something.
examples: Every method of dating fossils has [[inherent]] limits, so researchers often combine several.

lookalikes.tell: Inherent means built into something's nature; inherit means receive from someone who has died.

meaning: To prevent or reduce the development of a process.
examples: A coating of copper on a ship's hull can [[inhibit]] the growth of barnacles, keeping the hull smooth.

lookalikes.tell: Inhibit restrains; inhabit means live in a place.

meaning: Occurring first, before later changes or stages.
examples: The [[initial]] findings were revised after more tests.

lookalikes.tell: Initial means first; initiative is a plan or readiness to act.

meaning: Present from birth rather than learned; natural to a person or creature.
examples: Some linguists argue that children have an [[innate]] ability to learn grammar, since they master it long before anyone teaches them rules.

lookalikes.tell: Innate means inborn; inane means silly and pointless.

meaning: Using a new idea or method in a useful way.
examples: The project takes an [[innovative]] approach to cataloging artifacts.

lookalikes.tell: Innovative introduces a new approach; imitative copies an existing one.

meaning: Much greater than is usual or reasonable; excessive.
examples: Critics complained that the report devoted an [[inordinate]] amount of space to a single, minor study.
partners: an inordinate amount of time / attention

lookalikes.tell: Inordinate means excessive; subordinate means lower in rank.
Inordinate means excessive; an ordinate is a y-coordinate on a graph.

meaning: Eager to learn or to find out about things; sometimes, too curious about other people's affairs.
examples: An [[inquisitive]] child, she took apart the family clock to see how its gears turned.

lookalikes.tell: Inquisitive means curious; an inquisition is a harsh official investigation.
Inquisitive means eager to learn; acquisitive means eager to acquire possessions.

meaning: Harmful in a gradual, hidden way, so the damage is noticed only once it is serious.
examples: Lead poisoning is [[insidious]]: its early symptoms are so mild that a child may suffer lasting harm before anyone suspects the cause.

lookalikes.tell: Insidious means secretly harmful; invidious means unfair or likely to stir up resentment.

meaning: A clear and often fresh understanding of a difficult matter.
examples: The letters offer [[insight]] into the poet's revisions.

lookalikes.tell: Insight is understanding; incite means provoke action.

meaning: Having little effect or importance in the context.
examples: The measured difference was statistically [[insignificant]].

lookalikes.tell: Insignificant lacks importance; insufficient is not enough.

meaning: To hint at something unpleasant in an indirect, sly way.
examples: Without offering any proof, the columnist [[insinuated]] that the mayor had accepted bribes.

lookalikes.tell: Insinuate means hint at something slyly; instigate means start or provoke an action.

uses: In answer choices: "The reviewer insinuates that the scientist rushed her results into print."

meaning: Lacking flavor, energy or interest; bland.
examples: Reviewers praised the novel's setting but found its hero [[insipid]], a man with no desire strong enough to drive the plot.

lookalikes.tell: Insipid means dull and flavorless; incipient means just beginning.

meaning: Happening or done at once, with no delay.
examples: The telegraph made nearly [[instantaneous]] communication possible between cities hundreds of miles apart.

lookalikes.tell: Instantaneous means happening at once, with no delay; simultaneous means happening at the same time as something else.

meaning: To protect someone or something from outside influences or harm, such as heat, noise, or competition.
examples: Tariffs [[insulated]] the country's steelmakers from foreign competition, but they also raised prices for everyone who bought steel.

lookalikes.tell: Insulate means shield from outside effects; isolate means set apart from others.

meaning: Not physical; hard to touch, measure, or pin down.
examples: Beyond the salary, the job offered [[intangible]] rewards, such as the chance to work alongside the scientists she most admired.

lookalikes.tell: Intangible means not physical; intractable means hard to control or solve.

meaning: Necessary as a part of a larger thing.
examples: Public discussion was [[integral]] to the reform effort.

lookalikes.tell: Integral means essential; integer is a whole number.

meaning: To combine separate elements into a unified system.
short: fit parts into a larger whole
examples: The museum will [[integrate]] oral histories into the exhibit.

lookalikes.tell: Integrate unites parts; interrogate questions closely.

meaning: The quality of being honest and keeping to strong moral principles.
examples: Even her political rivals admired the judge's [[integrity]]: she had refused every gift and ruled against her own party more than once.
partners: personal integrity / a person of integrity

lookalikes.tell: Integrity is firm honesty or soundness; integration is the process of bringing parts or groups together.

meaning: To become or make something stronger in degree.
examples: The dispute may [[intensify]] as the deadline approaches.

lookalikes.tell: Intensify is an action; intensity names the degree of strength.

meaning: To step in on behalf of another person, especially to plead for them or to help settle a dispute.
examples: When the council threatened to close the school, the governor [[interceded]] and found money to keep it open.
partners: intercede on behalf of / with / for

lookalikes.tell: Intercede means step in for someone; intercept means stop something on its way.
Intercede means plead on someone's behalf; concede means admit or give up.

meaning: Able to substitute for each other without changing the result.
short: usable in place of one another
examples: The two terms are not [[interchangeable]] in this argument.

lookalikes.tell: Interchangeable means substitutable; interrelated means connected.

meaning: To get in the way of a process or activity, or to get involved where one is not wanted.
examples: Light from nearby cities can [[interfere]] with astronomers' observations of faint galaxies.

lookalikes.tell: Interfere means get in the way, often unwanted; intervene means step in, often to help or settle something.

meaning: Stopping and starting at irregular intervals.
examples: [[Intermittent]] rain slowed the harvest, with a few dry hours followed by sudden downpours.

lookalikes.tell: Intermittent means on and off; intermediate means in the middle.

meaning: To understand and describe what a text, event, or sign means.
examples: The historian [[interprets]] the speech in light of later letters.

lookalikes.tell: Interpret explains meaning; interrupt breaks the flow.

meaning: To become involved in a situation to change its course.
examples: Local leaders chose to [[intervene]] before the dispute grew.

lookalikes.tell: Intervene steps in to affect events; interview asks questions.

meaning: To suggest or hint at something indirectly, without stating it.
examples: In her letter, the duchess [[intimated]] that she might support the marriage, though she never said so outright.
The mayor [[intimated]] that more layoffs were coming.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The two sisters had always been close, so Jane noticed at once when Mary [[intimated]], in the lightest possible tone, that she might not come home for Christmas.
nearly.clue: in the lightest possible tone

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The ambassador never threatened war directly; he merely [[intimated]] that his government's patience had limits.
nearly.clue: never threatened war directly; he merely

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The early data [[intimated]] that the treatment might work, but the researchers were careful not to claim more until the full trial was complete.
nearly.clue: careful not to claim more until the full trial was complete

lookalikes.tell: Intimate means hint; intimidate means frighten someone into doing something.

meaning: Refusing to change one's views or to compromise at all.
examples: Talks collapsed after a week because both sides remained [[intransigent]], neither willing to give up a single demand.

lookalikes.tell: Intransigent means refusing to compromise; intransitive describes a verb that takes no object.

meaning: Fearless and adventurous, especially in facing danger.
examples: The [[intrepid]] reporter Nellie Bly traveled around the world in seventy-two days in 1889 and 1890.

lookalikes.tell: Intrepid means fearless; tepid means lukewarm or unenthusiastic.
Intrepid means without fear; trepidation means fear or nervousness.

meaning: Having many small, connected details.
examples: The drawing shows an [[intricate]] network of canals.

lookalikes.tell: Intricate has many details; intrinsic belongs to a thing's nature.

meaning: Having one's curiosity or interest strongly aroused.
examples: The archaeologist was [[intrigued]] by the strange markings on the pottery and spent months comparing them with ancient scripts.

lookalikes.tell: Intrigued means curious; intricate means having many small, detailed parts.

uses: In answer choices: "The narrator is intrigued by the stranger rather than frightened of him."

meaning: Part of the essential nature of something rather than added from outside.
examples: The poem's rhythm has [[intrinsic]] value apart from its subject.

lookalikes.tell: Intrinsic is inherent; intricate means complex in detail.

meaning: Never changing; always the same.
examples: The monks followed an [[invariable]] routine, rising at four and eating their single meal at noon every day for decades.

lookalikes.tell: Invariable means never changing; inevitable means certain to happen.

meaning: To give new energy, strength, or life to someone or something.
examples: A wave of young immigrant artists [[invigorated]] the city's music scene in the 1920s.
partners: invigorate the economy / a debate / the spirit

lookalikes.tell: Invigorate means give energy to; instigate means start or provoke something, often trouble.

meaning: To call on a rule, authority, or idea in an argument.
examples: The lawyer will [[invoke]] an earlier ruling in support of the claim.

lookalikes.tell: Invoke calls on authority; evoke calls up a memory or feeling.

meaning: Saying the opposite of what is meant, often for humor or criticism; also, describing a result that is the opposite of what was expected.
short: saying the opposite of what is meant
examples: The title “A Modest Proposal” is [[ironic]], since Swift's proposal is anything but modest.
In an [[ironic]] twist, the town's new fire station burned down that winter.

lookalikes.tell: Ironic means saying the opposite of what is meant; iconic means widely recognized as a symbol.

uses: In answer choices: "The author uses an ironic tone to criticize the town's celebration of its own generosity."

meaning: Not bearing on the matter being considered.
examples: The speaker dismissed the anecdote as [[irrelevant]] to the policy debate.

lookalikes.tell: Irrelevant is off-topic; irreverent lacks proper respect.

meaning: To separate something from its surroundings or other factors.
examples: The experiment aims to [[isolate]] the effect of light.
partners: isolate a variable / the effect of

lookalikes.tell: Isolate separates; insulate protects against heat or sound transfer.

meaning: Happening only in a few separate cases rather than widely; single and set apart.
examples: Officials insisted that the poisonings were [[isolated]] incidents, not signs of a problem across the whole water system.

lookalikes.tell: Isolated means set apart or occurring alone; insulated means protected from heat, noise, or outside influence.

meaning: Tired and no longer interested or excited, usually from having had too much of something.
examples: By his tenth year covering city politics, the reporter had grown [[jaded]], expecting every campaign promise to be broken.

lookalikes.tell: Jaded means tired of something from having too much of it; jagged means having sharp, uneven edges.

meaning: To put something in danger of harm or loss.
examples: A single careless mistake could [[jeopardize]] years of work on the vaccine.

lookalikes.tell: Jeopardize is the verb, to endanger; jeopardy is the noun, danger.

meaning: To throw away or abandon something that is no longer wanted; originally, to throw cargo overboard to lighten a ship or aircraft.
examples: Facing budget cuts, the agency [[jettisoned]] its plan for a second lunar mission.
partners: jettison a plan / cargo / an idea

lookalikes.tell: To jettison is to throw away; jetsam is the cargo thrown overboard that later washes ashore.

meaning: Showing good judgment and careful thought.
examples: A [[judicious]] use of pesticides, applied only where pests were found, saved the farm both money and bees.

lookalikes.tell: Judicious means wise; judicial means relating to courts and judges.

meaning: To show or argue that a decision, claim, or action is reasonable.
examples: The author uses data from three countries to [[justify]] her claim that the policy lowered costs.

lookalikes.tell: Justify argues that something is right; rectify makes a wrong thing right.

uses: In answer choices: "It justifies the researchers' choice of a small sample."

meaning: To place two things close together, often to show how they differ.
short: place side by side to compare
examples: The exhibit [[juxtaposes]] photographs of the harbor in 1900 and today, making the changes easy to see.

lookalikes.tell: Juxtapose places things side by side; superimpose places one on top of another.

uses: In answer choices: "The text juxtaposes two scientists' views of the same evidence."

meaning: Eager and enthusiastic about something.
examples: The young astronomer was [[keen]] to test her idea and spent every clear night at the telescope.

meaning: Sharp or highly sensitive; quick to notice or understand.
examples: A [[keen]] observer of city life, Jane Jacobs noticed patterns in sidewalk traffic that planners had missed.
Owls rely on [[keen]] hearing to find mice moving beneath the snow.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Young lab assistants were often eager, but what made Alvarez valuable was his [[keen]] eye: he could spot a hairline crack in a fossil that others had examined for hours.
nearly.clue: he could spot a hairline crack in a fossil

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The senator was admired for his eloquence, but his aides valued even more his [[keen]] ear for the weak point in an opponent's argument.
nearly.clue: for the weak point in an opponent's argument

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Emma, though eager for news, had a [[keen]] enough eye to see at once that her friend's cheerful letter hid some disappointment.
nearly.clue: to see at once that her friend's cheerful letter hid some disappointment

partners: a keen eye / keen hearing / a keen mind

lookalikes.tell: Keen here means sharp or acute; keening is loud wailing for the dead.

meaning: So full of twists, turns and connections that it is hard to find a way through, like a maze.
examples: Applicants had to navigate a [[labyrinthine]] permit process that sent them to six offices in three different buildings.

lookalikes.tell: Labyrinthine means confusingly complicated; laborious means requiring a lot of hard work.

meaning: Using very few words, sometimes to the point of seeming blunt or mysterious.
examples: Asked how the expedition had gone, the captain gave a [[laconic]] reply: "Cold. We turned back."

lookalikes.tell: Laconic means using few words; lackadaisical means lacking energy or care.

meaning: To express sorrow or regret about something.
examples: In the final chapter, the author [[laments]] the loss of the old forests, which she remembers from her childhood.
partners: lament the loss of / the decline of
uses: In answer choices: "The speaker laments the loss of a way of life."

meaning: To grow weak or fail to make progress, especially over a long time or in poor conditions.
examples: For decades the proposal [[languished]] in committee, never quite rejected but never brought to a vote.
partners: languish in obscurity / in prison / in committee

lookalikes.tell: To languish is to weaken or stall; anguish is severe pain or distress.

meaning: Generous giving of money or gifts, often by someone wealthy or powerful.
short: generous giving of gifts or money
examples: The new library was built with the [[largesse]] of a local merchant who had once been too poor to buy books.
partners: the largesse of a patron / government largesse

lookalikes.tell: Largesse is generous giving; largeness is simply great size.

meaning: Present but not yet active, visible or developed.
examples: The virus can remain [[latent]] in nerve cells for years before it causes any symptoms.

lookalikes.tell: Latent means hidden and not yet showing; patent means plainly obvious.

meaning: To praise someone or something highly, often in public.
examples: Critics [[lauded]] the novel for its unflinching portrait of life in a mining town.
partners: laud someone for something; widely lauded

lookalikes.tell: Laud means praise; loud means noisy.
Laud is the verb (praise); laudable describes something that deserves praise.

uses: In answer choices: "The author lauds the scientists for sharing their data freely."

meaning: Given or spent in great amounts; rich and costly.
short: generous or costly in the extreme
examples: The mill owner built a [[lavish]] mansion with forty rooms while his workers crowded into boardinghouses.
partners: lavish praise / a lavish feast / lavish spending

meaning: Not strict, careful, or firm enough.
examples: Investigators blamed [[lax]] inspections for the collapse, noting that the bridge had not been examined in six years.

lookalikes.tell: Lax means not strict; lacks means is missing something.

meaning: Offering or containing less than usual; meager, as in “lean years” or “a lean budget.”
examples: The farm barely survived the [[lean]] years of the drought.
The company kept a [[lean]] staff of only twelve people.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: During the [[lean]] winters of the 1780s, families in the valley survived on turnips and the little grain they had stored.
nearly.clue: survived on turnips and the little grain they had stored

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: In [[lean]] years, when acorns are scarce, the squirrels bury fewer nuts and raise fewer young.
nearly.clue: when acorns are scarce

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Resting his elbows on the fence, the old farmer described the [[lean]] seasons of his boyhood, when there was rarely meat on the table.
nearly.clue: when there was rarely meat on the table

partners: lean years / a lean budget / lean times

lookalikes.tell: Lean means meager; a lien is a legal claim on property until a debt is paid.

meaning: Suspicious or wary of something, and cautious about trusting it.
examples: Farmers who had lost money on earlier schemes were [[leery]] of the new irrigation company.

lookalikes.tell: Leery means wary; leering means looking at someone in an unpleasant, suggestive way.
Leery means distrustful; bleary means blurred or tired-looking, as eyes can be.

uses: In answer choices: "The narrator is leery of the stranger's offer of help."

meaning: Allowed by law or rules, or reasonable enough to be defended.
examples: The residents raised [[legitimate]] concerns about the plant, citing tests that showed lead in the water.

lookalikes.tell: Legitimate means lawful or justified; legislative relates to making laws.

meaning: Tolerant and merciful in punishing or judging; not strict.
examples: Because it was his first offense, the judge gave the teenager a [[lenient]] sentence of community service instead of jail.

meaning: Sluggish and lacking energy or enthusiasm.
examples: In the summer heat the lizards grew [[lethargic]], barely moving from the shade of the rocks.

lookalikes.tell: Lethargic means sluggish; lethal means deadly.

meaning: To use something one already has, such as a resource or an advantage, to gain as much as possible.
examples: The small nation [[leveraged]] its control of a key shipping strait to win better trade terms.
partners: leverage a resource / an advantage / expertise

lookalikes.tell: Leverage is the verb (make the most of an advantage); a lever is a bar used to move a load.
Leverage is power to gain an advantage; leeway is room or freedom to act.

meaning: To stay somewhere, or continue to exist, longer than expected, often slowly or reluctantly.
short: stay on; be slow to fade
examples: Doubts about the treaty [[lingered]] long after it was signed.
partners: doubts / smells / effects linger; linger over

lookalikes.tell: Linger means stay on; malinger means pretend to be sick to avoid work.
Linger means stay on; longer means of greater length.

meaning: Unwilling or reluctant to do something.
examples: The senator was [[loath]] to criticize the governor in public, since the two had campaigned together for years.
partners: loath to admit / loath to change

lookalikes.tell: Loath (an adjective) means unwilling; loathe (a verb) means hate.

meaning: To try to persuade officials or lawmakers to support a cause or law.
short: press officials to back a cause
examples: For a decade the nurses [[lobbied]] the state legislature to limit the number of patients assigned to each nurse.

meaning: Very talkative; fond of talking.
examples: The [[loquacious]] guide kept up a stream of stories, so the hikers learned more about the town's feuds than about its geology.

lookalikes.tell: Loquacious means talking a lot; eloquent means speaking well and persuasively.

meaning: Expressed clearly and easy to understand.
examples: Her [[lucid]] explanation of the tides made a complicated subject easy for visitors to follow.

lookalikes.tell: Lucid means clear; lurid means shocking or garishly bright.

meaning: Producing a great deal of money or profit.
examples: The fur trade proved so [[lucrative]] that rival companies built forts deep in the wilderness to control it.

lookalikes.tell: Lucrative means highly profitable; ludicrous means absurd enough to laugh at.

meaning: Generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful.
examples: In a [[magnanimous]] gesture, the victorious candidate invited her opponent to lead the new education council.
partners: magnanimous in victory / a magnanimous gesture

lookalikes.tell: Magnanimous means generous and forgiving; unanimous means agreed on by everyone.

meaning: To keep something in its existing state or in good working order.
examples: The village paid a keeper to [[maintain]] the lighthouse and its lamp.

meaning: To state firmly that something is true, especially when others disagree.
examples: Throughout the trial, the defendant [[maintained]] that he had never met the victim.
Some linguists [[maintain]] that all human languages share a hidden common structure.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The ship's owners had spent heavily to keep the vessel in repair, and after the wreck they [[maintained]] that she had been perfectly seaworthy; the inquiry found otherwise.
nearly.clue: the inquiry found otherwise

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Critics blamed a faulty instrument, but the physicist, who had serviced the detector herself, [[maintained]] that the signal was real, and in 1998 a larger detector proved her right.
nearly.clue: that the signal was real

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Old Mr. Fenn kept his garden in perfect order, and he [[maintained]] to anyone who would listen that his roses were the finest in the county.
nearly.clue: to anyone who would listen that his roses were the finest

lookalikes.tell: Maintain here means claim firmly; sustain means keep something going.

uses: In answer choices: "The author maintains that the treaty succeeded despite its critics."

meaning: Wishing to do harm or evil to others.
examples: In the old tale, a [[malevolent]] spirit lured travelers off the mountain path and into the fog.

lookalikes.tell: Malevolent means wishing harm; malleable means easily shaped or influenced.

meaning: Intending to hurt or harm someone.
examples: The editor apologized for printing a [[malicious]] rumor that had no basis in fact.

lookalikes.tell: Malicious describes intent to harm; malignant describes something harmful that spreads, such as a tumor.

meaning: Easily shaped or bent; of a person or an idea, easily influenced or changed.
short: easily shaped, as metal or opinion
examples: Studies suggest that memory is more [[malleable]] than most people assume, since details can shift each time an event is recalled.
Gold is so [[malleable]] that a single ounce can be hammered into a sheet thinner than a strand of hair.

lookalikes.tell: Malleable means easily shaped; malevolent means wishing harm on others.

meaning: Able to be dealt with or controlled without too much difficulty.
examples: Breaking the survey into ten short sections made the workload [[manageable]] for the volunteers.

lookalikes.tell: Manageable means able to be handled; malleable means able to be shaped.

meaning: To show or reveal a quality or condition clearly.
examples: The disease can take years to [[manifest]] itself, so early testing is important.

lookalikes.tell: Manifest means show clearly; a manifesto is a public statement of aims.

meaning: Small in amount or effect, or at the edge of something.
examples: The new fertilizer produced only a [[marginal]] increase in yield, too small to justify its cost.

lookalikes.tell: Marginal means small or at the edge; marginalize means push someone to the edge of a group.

meaning: Clear and noticeable; easy to see or detect.
examples: There was a [[marked]] improvement in the patients who received the drug.
Her second novel shows a [[marked]] change in style.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Each of the tagged fish carried a numbered label, and those raised in cooler water showed a [[marked]] difference in growth: they were nearly twice as long after a year.
nearly.clue: they were nearly twice as long after a year

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Maps drawn after the survey show a [[marked]] shift in the border, which moved almost forty miles to the west.
nearly.clue: which moved almost forty miles to the west

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: After her brother's return, there was a [[marked]] change in Anne's manner: she laughed often and no longer hid in the library.
nearly.clue: she laughed often and no longer hid in the library

lookalikes.tell: Marked means clearly noticeable; marred means damaged or spoiled.

meaning: Too small in amount to be enough.
examples: Living on a [[meager]] salary, the young teacher often skipped lunch so she could buy books for her students.

lookalikes.tell: Meager means too small in amount; eager means keen and enthusiastic.

meaning: Careful, calm, and restrained rather than extreme.
examples: Rather than attacking her critics, the scientist gave a [[measured]] reply that addressed each objection in turn.

lookalikes.tell: Measured means careful and restrained; measurable means able to be measured.

uses: In answer choices: "The author's tone is measured, weighing both sides before reaching a judgment."

meaning: To help two opposing sides reach an agreement or settle a dispute.
examples: A retired judge was asked to [[mediate]] between the city and the striking transit workers.
partners: mediate a dispute / a conflict / between sides

lookalikes.tell: Mediate means help settle a dispute; meditate means think quietly and deeply.
Mediate means negotiate between sides; medicate means treat with medicine.

meaning: Only ordinary or moderate in quality; not very good.
examples: The restaurant's reviews were [[mediocre]], praising the view over the harbor but calling the food forgettable.

lookalikes.tell: Mediocre describes ordinary quality; meager describes a small or insufficient amount.

meaning: Having or causing a deep, quiet sadness, often without a clear cause.
examples: The poem's [[melancholy]] final stanza, in which the speaker watches the geese fly south, contrasts with the bright summer scenes before it.

lookalikes.tell: Melancholy means quietly sad; melodramatic means exaggerated and overly emotional.

uses: In answer choices: "The tone of the passage shifts from hopeful to melancholy."

meaning: Pleasantly soft, smooth, or relaxed, without harshness. Of a person, it means calm and easygoing, often with age.
examples: The cello's [[mellow]] tone filled the hall without overwhelming the singers.

lookalikes.tell: Mellow means soft and smooth; mallow is a plant.

meaning: To threaten or put in danger. As a noun, a menace is a threat.
examples: Invasive zebra mussels now [[menace]] native mussel species throughout the Great Lakes.
partners: menace wildlife / crops / a menace to

lookalikes.tell: To menace is to threaten; menial describes lowly, unskilled work.

meaning: Changing moods or opinions suddenly and unpredictably.
examples: The composer was famously [[mercurial]], charming his musicians one morning and storming out of rehearsal the next.

lookalikes.tell: Mercurial means moody and unpredictable; mercenary means motivated only by money.

meaning: Very fast and dramatic, like a meteor, especially of a rise to success.
short: extremely rapid, as of a rise
examples: The company's [[meteoric]] rise, from a garage workshop to a thousand employees in four years, surprised even its founders.

lookalikes.tell: Meteoric means dazzlingly fast; meteorological means having to do with weather.

meaning: Done carefully in a set order, step by step; of a person, working in an orderly way.
examples: Her [[methodical]] notes, dated and numbered page by page, allowed later scientists to repeat every one of her trials.

lookalikes.tell: Methodical means orderly and careful; methodological means relating to the methods a study uses.

meaning: Showing great care and attention to every detail.
examples: A [[meticulous]] record keeper, the botanist noted the date, weather, and place of every specimen she collected.

meaning: To copy the look, sound or behavior of someone or something, sometimes to make fun of it.
examples: Some harmless hoverflies [[mimic]] the yellow and black stripes of wasps, so birds leave them alone.
partners: mimic the appearance of / mimic natural conditions

lookalikes.tell: To mimic is to copy something; to mime is to act something out without words.

meaning: To make something seem less important or serious than it really is. It can also mean to reduce something to the smallest possible amount.
short: play down, or keep as small as possible
examples: The company's statement [[minimized]] the leak, calling it a minor spill, even though it had closed three beaches.
partners: minimize the risk / minimize a problem
uses: In answer choices: "The author minimizes the importance of the delay by calling it routine."

meaning: Extremely small.
examples: The sensor can detect [[minuscule]] traces of lead, as little as a few parts per billion.

lookalikes.tell: Minuscule means tiny; minutiae are small, trivial details.

meaning: Extremely small; also, very careful and detailed.
examples: The camera can detect [[minute]] changes in the color of a leaf.
Only [[minute]] amounts of the metal were found in the soil.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The sensor takes a reading every second and records vibrations so [[minute]] that no person standing on the bridge could feel them.
nearly.clue: that no person standing on the bridge could feel them

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The forger's copy was nearly perfect; only a [[minute]] difference in the curl of one letter, visible under a magnifying glass, gave it away.

nearly.text: Because the study was paid for by the sugar industry, some nutritionists considered its authors [[partial]], and they asked independent labs to repeat the work.
nearly.clue: paid for by the sugar industry

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Grandmother insisted that she loved all six grandchildren equally, but everyone knew she was [[partial]] to Ellen, who got the largest slice of every pie.
nearly.clue: who got the largest slice of every pie

lookalikes.tell: Partial means favoring one side in a judgment; partisan means loyal to a party or cause, often blindly.

meaning: Strongly supporting one party or cause, often without fair consideration of other views.
examples: The historian warned that the pamphlet, written by the governor's own campaign staff, gave a [[partisan]] account of the election.

lookalikes.tell: Partisan means biased toward one side; an artisan is a skilled craftsperson.

meaning: Accepting events without taking action.
examples: In many early films, women were cast in [[passive]] roles, waiting to be rescued rather than acting on their own.

lookalikes.tell: Passive means not taking action; pensive means deep in thought.

meaning: Completely obvious; clear to anyone who looks.
everyday: a legal right to an invention
examples: The claim was a [[patent]] falsehood, easily disproved by the records.
Her discomfort was [[patent]] to everyone at the table.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The inventor's application was rejected for a [[patent]] reason: a nearly identical machine had been on sale for a decade.
nearly.clue: a nearly identical machine had been on sale for a decade

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The treaty's unfairness was [[patent]]: one side gave up half its territory and received nothing in return.
nearly.clue: one side gave up half its territory and received nothing in return

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: His boredom at the recital was [[patent]]; he yawned openly and checked his watch every few minutes.
nearly.clue: he yawned openly and checked his watch every few minutes

lookalikes.tell: Patent means obvious; potent means powerful.

meaning: To treat someone as less capable or informed.
examples: The guidebook's author tried not to [[patronize]] readers, assuming they could follow a detailed map.

lookalikes.tell: To patronize someone is to talk down to them; a patron is a supporter or a regular customer, and to patronize a shop is only to shop there.

meaning: The state of being present in only small, or too small, amounts; scarcity.
examples: The [[paucity]] of written records from the period forces historians to rely on archaeology.
partners: a paucity of evidence / data / information

lookalikes.tell: A paucity is a shortage of something; a pauper is a very poor person.
A paucity is a shortage; paltry is an adjective describing an amount that is small and worthless.

meaning: Distinctive or unusual in a noticeable way.
examples: The ornithologist noticed a [[peculiar]] habit: the birds buried their eggs in warm volcanic sand.

meaning: Belonging to or found in only one person, place, group or thing; usually used as “peculiar to.”
examples: The clicking sounds [[peculiar]] to several southern African languages are rare elsewhere in the world.
Each valley developed farming customs [[peculiar]] to its own soil and climate.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The lizards on the island have a blue tongue [[peculiar]] to that population; no other members of the species, on the mainland or elsewhere, share it.
nearly.clue: no other members of the species, on the mainland or elsewhere, share it

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The town's charter granted rights [[peculiar]] to its citizens, such as the right to fish the royal river, which no other town in the kingdom enjoyed.
nearly.clue: which no other town in the kingdom enjoyed

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Grandfather had a laugh [[peculiar]] to himself, a dry wheeze that none of his children inherited and that the whole family could recognize from two rooms away.
nearly.clue: that none of his children inherited

partners: peculiar to a region / a species

lookalikes.tell: Peculiar to means belonging only to; pecuniary means having to do with money.

meaning: Too concerned with minor details, rules or showing off one's learning.
short: fussy about minor details or rules
examples: Students found the lecturer [[pedantic]]: he spent the first hour correcting the spelling of Latin plant names instead of explaining why the plants mattered.

lookalikes.tell: Pedantic means fussy about details and rules; pedagogical means relating to teaching.

meaning: Ordinary and uninspired; lacking imagination or excitement.
examples: Critics called the film's plot [[pedestrian]], though they admired its photography.
Her early poems are [[pedestrian]]; only in her forties did she find her voice.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The novelist's descriptions of busy city streets, crowded with walkers and carriages, are vivid enough, but his dialogue is [[pedestrian]], and every character sounds the same.
nearly.clue: every character sounds the same

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The grant committee dismissed the proposal to count foot traffic on city sidewalks as [[pedestrian]]; it wanted bolder, more original research.
nearly.clue: it wanted bolder, more original research

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Historians once dismissed the diary as [[pedestrian]], a dull record of weather and prices, until they realized how much those prices revealed about the war's effects.
nearly.clue: a dull record of weather and prices

lookalikes.tell: Pedestrian means dull (or on foot); pediatric means relating to children's medicine.

meaning: To become aware of something through the senses or the mind.
examples: Bees [[perceive]] ultraviolet light, which reveals patterns on flowers that people cannot see.

lookalikes.tell: Perceive means become aware of; conceive means form an idea.

meaning: Able to notice and understand subtle details.
examples: In a [[perceptive]] review, the critic noticed that every chapter ends with the same image of a closing door.

meaning: Lasting for a very long time, or coming back again and again.
short: lasting or recurring year after year
examples: Flooding is a [[perennial]] problem in the delta, returning with the spring rains nearly every year.

lookalikes.tell: Perennial means lasting or recurring year after year; biennial means happening every two years.

meaning: Done quickly and with little care or interest, only because it has to be done.
examples: The inspector gave the ship a [[perfunctory]] glance, stamped the papers, and waved it into port.

lookalikes.tell: Perfunctory means done carelessly as a routine; peremptory means insisting on immediate obedience.

meaning: Less central to the main issue.
examples: The report treats cost as a [[peripheral]] issue, focusing instead on the program's effects on students.

meaning: To spread through every part of something.
examples: A sense of loss [[permeates]] the novel, from its opening funeral to its final, empty house.
partners: permeate a culture / permeate the soil

lookalikes.tell: Permeate means spread throughout; perpetrate means carry out something wrong, such as a crime.

meaning: Having a harmful effect, especially one that develops gradually or in a way that is not easily noticed.
short: harmful, often in a hidden way
examples: The report described misinformation as [[pernicious]] because it spread quietly long before anyone noticed the damage.

lookalikes.tell: Pernicious means harmful; persnickety means fussy about small details.
Pernicious means harmful; permissive means allowing a lot of freedom.

meaning: Never ending or changing; lasting forever, or happening so often that it seems endless.
examples: Families in the valley lived in [[perpetual]] fear of floods until the dam was built.

lookalikes.tell: Perpetual is the adjective (never-ending); perpetuate is the verb (keep something going).
Perpetual means never-ending; perceptual means related to perception.

meaning: To cause a condition or practice to continue.
examples: Critics argued that the textbooks [[perpetuate]] old myths about the region by repeating them without comment.

meaning: Confused and unable to understand something.
short: troubled at being unable to understand
examples: Astronomers were [[perplexed]] by the star's irregular dimming, which fit no known pattern.
The letter left her [[perplexed]]: it was signed by a cousin she had never heard of.

lookalikes.tell: Perplexed means confused; vexed means annoyed.

uses: In answer choices: "The narrator is perplexed by her mentor's sudden change of heart."

meaning: To keep trying to do something in spite of difficulty or delay.
examples: Though her first three grant applications were rejected, the biologist [[persevered]] and won funding on her fourth attempt.

lookalikes.tell: To persevere is to keep trying; to preserve is to keep something safe or unchanged.

meaning: To continue to exist, or to keep doing something despite difficulty.
examples: The drought [[persisted]] for seven years, forcing many families to leave the valley.

lookalikes.tell: Persist means keep going; insist means demand firmly.

meaning: Good at convincing someone to believe or do something.
examples: The lawyer's most [[persuasive]] evidence was a simple chart showing that wages had fallen while profits rose.

lookalikes.tell: Persuasive means convincing; pervasive means spread throughout.

meaning: Directly related to the matter being discussed.
short: directly to the point at hand
examples: The judge ruled that the letters were [[pertinent]] to the case, since they showed what the defendant knew about the contract.

lookalikes.tell: Pertinent means relevant; impertinent means rude or disrespectful.

meaning: Anxious, worried, or unsettled, especially because of something unexpected.
examples: The captain was [[perturbed]] to find that the compass readings no longer matched the stars.

lookalikes.tell: Perturbed means worried or upset; perplexed means puzzled.

uses: In answer choices: "The narrator is perturbed by her brother's sudden silence."

meaning: To read or examine something carefully and in detail. In casual speech it is often used to mean "skim," but the careful sense is the traditional one.
examples: The archivist [[perused]] every page of the ship's log, searching for any mention of the storm.

lookalikes.tell: Peruse means read carefully; pursue means chase or strive for.

meaning: Spread throughout a place, group, or system.
examples: The survey found that concern about water quality was [[pervasive]], appearing in nearly every town in the region.

meaning: Tending to expect bad outcomes.
examples: Early reports were [[pessimistic]], predicting that the species would vanish within a decade.
uses: In answer choices: "The report is pessimistic about the species' chances of recovery."

meaning: Done a little at a time, in separate stages, rather than all at once or by an overall plan.
short: bit by bit, not all at once
examples: Instead of passing one sweeping law, the council made [[piecemeal]] changes to the zoning code over twenty years.

lookalikes.tell: Piecemeal means done bit by bit; piecework is work paid for by the item produced.

meaning: Being among the first to develop a new idea, method or field.
examples: Her [[pioneering]] work on radioactivity opened a field that dozens of later physicists would build on.

meaning: Short but full of meaning and force.
examples: Franklin's almanac was known for [[pithy]] sayings such as "Well done is better than well said."

lookalikes.tell: Pithy means brief and meaningful; pity means sympathy for someone's suffering.

meaning: Of central importance, especially in causing a turning point.
examples: The 1954 ruling played a [[pivotal]] role in ending segregation in American schools.

lookalikes.tell: Pivotal marks a turning point; vital means needed to keep something alive or working.

meaning: To make someone less angry, often by giving them something they want.
short: soothe anger with a small concession
examples: To [[placate]] the striking workers, the owners offered a small raise, though not the shorter hours they had demanded.

lookalikes.tell: Placate means calm someone who is angry; placid means already calm and peaceful.

meaning: Calm and peaceful, with little movement or excitement.
examples: The lake was [[placid]] at dawn, but by noon the wind had whipped it into whitecaps.

lookalikes.tell: Placid means calm; placate means calm someone who is angry.
Placid means calm; flaccid means soft and limp.

meaning: Easily shaped or changed; able to be molded, as clay or a young brain is.
examples: The brain remains [[plastic]] throughout life, forming new connections as we learn.
Wet clay is [[plastic]]; once fired, it becomes rigid.
